04_marg1033: Morally. If Joseph dies in you, that is, if you take up in yourself the mortification of Christ and mortify your members to sin, the children of Israel are multiplied in you, that is, good and spiritual senses. 04_marg1034: ORIGEN. Allegorically. This is the devil, who “said in his heart: There is no God”; who says to his people, that is, to the apostate angels: “Behold the people of the children of Israel,” etc., that is, of those who can see God with the mind; “it is mightier than we; come, let us wisely oppress it.” The devil perceives that the people of Israel is great and stronger than he, because he has often fought with it and is often overcome. He knows that Jacob wrestled, and by the help of an angel prevailed against the adversary and was strong with God. He perceived too the wrestlings of other saints and endured spiritual combats; he fears lest a war should some day come and they should side with his adversaries, and, having overcome them, depart from his land. It seems to me, from what had been shown to the patriarchs and prophets about the coming of Christ, that he perceives that one is coming who will strip off his principalities and powers, and triumph over them confidently, and afflict them on the wood of the cross.

04_marg1036: All the kings of the Egyptians were formerly called Pharaos, as now the Ptolemies, and the Arsacids the kings of the Persians, and the Caesars Augusti of the Romans. 04_marg1037: Morally. First I wish to ask who is the king in Egypt who knows Joseph, and who does not. For while he reigned who knew Joseph, the children of Israel are not said to have been afflicted, nor worn out in clay and brick, nor their males killed and the females kept alive; but when he began to reign who did not know Joseph. If the Lord rules us, and the sense of our mind or soul is enlightened by God, remembering that Christ rose from the dead, in Egypt, that is, in our flesh, our spirit holds the kingdom with justice, and does not wear out the children of Israel, that is, the rational senses or the virtues, in clay and brick, nor grind them down with earthly cares. If our sense loses the memory of these things and does not know Christ, then “the wisdom of the flesh,” which “is an enemy to God,” succeeds to the kingdom. It addresses its people, that is, the bodily pleasures, and, calling the leaders of the vices to counsel, deliberates against the children of Israel how they may be got round, oppressed, afflicted with clay and brick; how they may expose the males and rear the females; how they may build the cities of Egypt and its fortified cities. Nor is it to be thought that the divine books tell the deeds of the Egyptians without cause; but “what things were written, were written for our learning”; so that you who hear these things, if perhaps you are baptized and numbered among the children of Israel, and have received the Lord as king in yourself, and after this wish to turn aside and do the works of the world, to carry out the deeds of the earth and the services of clay, may know that another king has risen in you who does not know Joseph, a king of Egypt. He compels you to his works, to work brick and clay. He, with masters and taskmasters set over you, drives you with whips to earthly works, so that you may build cities for him. He makes you run about the world, troubling the elements of sea and land for greed; beat at the courts with lawsuits; weary your neighbours with quarrels for a little turf of land; lay snares for chastity, deceive innocence, commit foul things at home, cruel things abroad, shameful things within the conscience. In things of this kind know that you are serving as a soldier of the king of Egypt, which is to be driven by the spirit of this world.

04_marg1038: Therefore he set over them masters, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. The devil, having called his people together, desires to oppress the rational sense, which is now called Israel in figure. He set over them masters of works, to compel them to learn the works of the flesh; according to that: “They were mingled among the heathens, and learned their works.” He teaches them to build cities for Pharao: Phithom, which signifies “mouth of failing” or “of the abyss”; and Ramesses, which is “the stirring of the moth”; and On, that is, Heliopolis, which is called the city of the sun. The mouth fails from truth and proofs when it speaks a lie. He was a liar from the beginning, and therefore wishes such cities to be built for him. “Mouth of the abyss,” because the abyss is the place of his perdition. His other city is “the stirring of the moth.” For whoever follows him lays up treasure where the moth destroys and thieves break through and steal. He builds also the city of the sun, under a false name, because “he transformeth himself into an angel of light.” In these he busies the minds that were made to see God. Yet he foresees that wars threaten him and that the ruin of his people is ripe. Therefore he says: “The people of Israel is stronger than we.” Would that he might feel us too to be stronger than he: that is, that I may not receive the evil thoughts and desires he sends in, but drive back his fiery darts with the shield of faith, and in all that he suggests say: “Begone, Satan; for it is written: The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve.” And as for his saying, “Lest perhaps a war befall us, and these side with our adversaries”: from the prophetic voices he foresees the war to come, and that he must be forsaken by the children of Israel, and that they will side with his adversary and be added to the Lord. This is what Jeremias says: “The partridge hath cried, she hath gathered together what she did not bring forth; he hath gathered riches, and not by right; in the midst of his days he shall leave them, and in his latter end he shall be a fool.” So he understands that he is the partridge that gathered what she did not bring forth, and that those whom he gathered without right will leave him and follow Christ, who begot them. He will remain a fool, when the whole creation flees to its maker and parent. Therefore he is indignant, saying: “Lest, overcoming us, they go out of our land.” He does not wish us to go out of his land, so that we may always bear the image of the earthly; lest, leaving him, we flee to him who has prepared the kingdom of heaven, leaving “the image of the earthly” and taking up “the image of the heavenly.” Therefore he set up masters of works, to teach their arts and make us craftsmen of malice. And because there are many masters of malice whom Pharao set over us, who command, exact and wring out earthly works, therefore, when Christ came, he made other teachers fighting against them, who, subduing all their principalities, powers and virtues, might defend the children of Israel from violence, and teach them the works of Israel and to see God with the mind; to leave the works of Pharao, to go out of the land of Egypt, to put off the ways of Egypt and the whole old man with his deeds, and to put on the new, who according to God is created.

04_marg1040: And the king of Egypt spoke, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. We find these things not only in the world, which is spiritually called Egypt, but in each one of us. The prince of this world does not wish the males to be kept alive, but the females. In the female the flesh and the affections of the flesh are signified; but the male is the rational sense and the intellectual spirit, which can grasp heavenly things, understand God, seek the things that are above. This the prince of Egypt hates and desires to be killed; but he desires the things of the flesh to live, and what belongs to bodily matter, not only to live but to be increased and cultivated. For he wishes all to savour fleshly things, to seek temporal things and those upon the earth; that no one lift his eyes to heaven, no one ask whence he came here, no one remember his country, paradise. So when you see men leading their lives in pleasures, floating in luxury, giving themselves to feasts and lewdness, know that in them the king of Egypt is killing the males and keeping the females alive. But if he sees one in a thousand turned to God, lifting his eyes upward, seeking eternal things, hating delights and luxury, loving continence, this one Pharao desires to be killed as a male; he persecutes him, attacks him with a thousand engines; he hates such men, and does not let them live in Egypt. Hence it is that in this world the servants of God are held in contempt and exposed to insults; hence hatreds and persecutions are stirred up against them.
04_marg1041: ORIGEN. He tries also to corrupt the midwives, of whom one was called Sephora, that is, “sparrow,” the other Phua, that is, “red” or “modest”; through them he seeks to have the males killed and the females kept alive. “But the midwives feared God, and did not as he commanded them.” The midwives taught us beforehand to hold a certain form of rational learning. For midwives are physicians, and they tend both the males and the females being born. So common learning is rational knowledge, and it reaches almost every sense, instructs and tends all. If anyone in it is of manly mind, who wishes to seek heavenly things and pursue divine things, he will come, as one doctored and strong, more ready through these learnings to the understanding of divine things. For there is one, like the sparrow, which teaches loftier things and calls upward on the wings of rational teaching. The other, red or modest, is moral: it orders conduct, teaches modesty and uprightness. Yet to me, because Scripture says of them that they feared God and did not do the command of the king of Egypt, they seem to keep the figure of both Testaments; and Sephora, which is interpreted “sparrow,” seems to fit the Law, which is spiritual; and Phua, which is “red” or “modest,” to point to the Gospels, which are red with the blood of Christ and glow red through the whole world with the blood of the passion. By these, then, as by midwives, the souls that are born in the Church are tended, because all the medicines of learning are supplied from the Scriptures. Yet Pharao tries through them to kill the males, when he suggests heresies and wicked doctrines to those studious in the divine Scriptures. But the foundation of God stands firm. For the midwives fear God, that is, they teach the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. So what follows fits more aptly: because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses. Which according to the letter has no consequence; for a house is not made because God is feared. But if you see how the Scriptures of the New and Old Testament, teaching the fear of God, make the houses of the Church and fill the whole world with houses of prayer, it will seem reasonably written. So these midwives, because they fear God, that is, teach the fear of God, do not do the command of the king of Egypt, but keep the males alive; and yet it is not said that they obeyed by keeping the females alive. And I say confidently: they do not keep the females alive. For neither vices nor luxury are taught in the Church, nor are sins nourished, which Pharao wants when he orders the females to be kept alive; but virtue alone is cultivated and nourished. But let us refer these things to each one. If you fear God, you do not do the command of the king of Egypt; for he commands you to live in delights and to covet present things. You, if you fear God and perform the office of a midwife, if you desire to bring salvation to your soul, keep the males alive; that is, you tend and nurse the inner man who is in you, and by good deeds and understandings gain eternal life.

04_marg1044: They answered, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether such lies are approved by divine authority, because it is written that God dealt well with the midwives. But whether God pardoned the lies for the sake of the mercy, or judged even the lie worthy of reward, is uncertain. For the midwives did one thing in keeping the little ones alive, another in lying to Pharao. In keeping them alive it was a work of mercy; but they used the lie for themselves, lest Pharao harm them, which could belong not to praise but to pardon. Nor is authority for lying given from this to those of whom it is said: “And in their mouth there was found no lie.” For the life of some, far below the profession of the saints, if it has these sins of lies, is borne with for its very progress and disposition, especially if they do not yet know how to wait for heavenly benefits, but are busied about earthly ones. But those whose “conversation is in heaven” I do not think ought to shape the measure of their tongue concerning truth and falsehood by the example of the midwives.
04_marg1045: GREGORY. Lying must be shunned with the greatest care, though it is of lighter guilt if someone lies in doing a kindness. But since it is written, “The mouth that belieth killeth the soul,” and “Thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie,” the perfect flee even this, so that not even anyone’s life is defended by their deceit, lest they harm their own soul while striving to profit another’s flesh; though we readily believe that this kind of sin is forgiven. For if any guilt whatever is purged by a following devout work, how much more easily is this wiped away, which piety, the mother of good work, accompanies? But many try to assert from the deceit of the midwives that this kind of lie is not a sin, because the Lord built them houses. In which recompense, rather, it is known what the guilt of a lie deserves. For the reward of their kindness, which could have been repaid in eternal life, was turned aside, for the guilt of the lie, into an earthly recompense; so that in their life, which they wished to protect by lying, they received the good they had done, and had no further reward of wages to wait for. For if it is weighed closely, they lied for love of the present life, not with the intention of a reward. For by sparing they tried to shield the life of the infants; by lying, their own.

04_marg1046: In the book of Expressions. “And because the midwives feared God, he built them houses.” Did they not have houses before? Or does this word belong to riches, or rather to some suitable means of household goods? For it seems like what Jacob said to his father-in-law: “Now when shall I too make a house for myself?” For he had said that Laban’s cattle had increased under him, which Laban himself confessed, saying: “God hath blessed me at thy coming.” So “as you too” is understood; for this is what “I too” seems to mean; so that it seems to belong to the making of the house itself that the wages to be fixed are then proposed by Laban.

04_marg1047: Pharao therefore charged, etc. ORIGEN. Morally. The Egyptians, whom Pharao charges here, keep only the females alive and hate the males; for they hated the virtues and nourished the vices. Now too the Egyptians lie in wait, if a male is born to the Hebrews, to kill it at once, unless they take care, watch and hide it. Scripture tells that one of the tribe of Levi begot a male, and saw that the infant was goodly, and hid him. So let us not do our justice before men, but with the door shut pray to our Father in secret, and let not the left hand know what the right hand does; lest it be snatched away by the Egyptians, seized, and drowned in the waves. If I give alms because it is a work of God, I beget a male. But if I seek praise from men and do not hide it, it is snatched away by the Egyptians and drowned in the river; and with so much labour and so much zeal I have begotten a male for the Egyptians.

04_marg1048: After this there went, etc. RABANUS. Hence Josephus says: But Amram, fearing that if caught he would fall to the king’s wrath, and himself perish with the boy and shut out the providence of God, decided rather to see to the boy’s safety in this way, and judged that this was the providence of hiding. He prepared a round vessel woven of withies, of about the size of a cradle, enough for the infant to lie in it roomily. Then they daubed it with pitch; for it is the nature of pitch to keep back the entry of water in wicker vessels. So putting the infant there, and setting it near the river, they left his safety to God. Now Thermuth was the king’s daughter. While she was playing by the bank of the river, seeing that vessel carried by the river, she ordered that cradle to be brought to her. When those who had been sent for this came with the cradle, she took it, and seeing the infant, rejoiced greatly at his size and beauty. For God used such care about Moses that by the very people who, because of his birth, had decreed to destroy the whole race of the Hebrews, he was held worthy of food and care. And Thermuth, the king’s daughter, ordered a woman to be brought to give the infant the breast. When he would not go to her breasts but shunned them, and did this with many women, Mary, standing by what was being done, as if she seemed to be standing among the others by chance, said: In vain, O queen, do you call these women to nurse the infant, who have no kinship with him. But if you order one of the Hebrew women to be brought, I think he will be able to take the breast as from one of his own tribe. And when she was thought to have spoken well, she ordered her to go and bring someone who could suckle him. And she, having received such leave, came back bringing her mother, known to no one. And the infant went gladly, as it were, to her breasts; and at the queen’s request the nursing of the boy was entrusted to her with all diligence. And according to the outcome of events the name was given him because he was saved from the river. For the Egyptians call water moy, and saved ses; so putting this together from both they gave him the name Moses, that is, “saved from the water.” Allegorically. The parents of Moses, whose faith and works the natural law adorned, are the patriarchs, from whom Moses himself and those who received the law of the letter were born. So Moses, born in his parents’ house, is hidden for three months, since the old law lay hidden among the Jewish people for three periods before the coming of Christ, that is, under the judges, under the kings, under the priests, until he came who gave the law and handed it over to the Gentiles through the whole breadth of the world, to be kept spiritually. And Pharao’s daughter is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which, though she now rejoices in a true parent, that is, God the Father, yet before, when she served idols, followed another father; of whom it was said to her by the divine voice in the Psalm: “Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thy ear; and forget thy people and thy father’s house,” etc. So she went out of her father’s house and came to the waters of baptism, to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house; and coming to baptism she received the law, which was then inside a basket of bulrushes, woven of many twigs or of papyrus and daubed with pitch and slime, because it was fouled, hemmed in by the cheap and earthly traditions of the Jews; until the Church took it up from the marshy and muddy places of fleshly senses, and within the halls of true wisdom and the royal roofs. It spent its infancy among its own, that is, among those who did not know how to understand it spiritually, a little thing and the food of sucklings. But when it came to the Church and was rightly understood through her, it was made stronger. What then is it that she who nursed the boy received wages from Pharao’s daughter, unless that the synagogue, with whom the law was born and nursed, received this wage from the Church: that it should no longer worship idols; seeing those from the Gentiles who had believed so turned to the Lord that they utterly rejected images and no longer worshipped them, it too is taught to blush at worshipping idols?
04_marg1049: And seeing him a goodly child, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. Pharao’s daughter is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, to whom it is said through the Prophet: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house, for the king hath greatly desired thy beauty.” This, then, is she who went out of her father’s house and came to the waters to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house; and at once she received bowels of mercy and had pity on the infant. Coming into the marsh, she found Moses lying, exposed by his own people, and had him nursed. He is nursed among his own and spends his infancy there; grown stronger, he is brought to her and adopted as a son. Moses signifies the Law. So the Church, coming to the waters of baptism, received the Law shut in a thibis and daubed with pitch. Now a thibis is a covering woven of papyrus and twigs, or formed from the bark of trees. So the Law lay shut within coverings of this kind, daubed with pitch and slime, that is, with the cheap and foul senses of the Jews; it lay fouled and smeared until the Church came from the Gentiles and took it up from the muddy and marshy places into the halls of wisdom and the royal roofs. Yet it spends its infancy among its own; for among those who do not understand it spiritually it is little, an infant, and has the food of sucklings. When it comes to the Church, Moses is stronger and more vigorous; for when the veil of the letter is removed, perfect food is found in the reading of it. She receives the wages of nursing from Pharao’s daughter, with whom the law is born and nursed. But what is it that the synagogue receives from the Church? I think it is what Moses says: “I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will anger you.” So the synagogue receives this wage from the Church: that it no longer worships idols. For seeing the Gentiles so turned to God that they no longer know idols, it blushes to worship idols any longer. We too, if we have had Pharao for a father, if he begot us in evil works, when we come to the waters, let us take up the law of God. Let not the letters seem foul to us like a dark covering; let us eat what in it is little and for sucklings; let us take up what is perfect and place it within the royal roofs of the heart. We have a great and strong Moses: let us think nothing small of him, nothing cheap, but all magnificent, all excellent, all goodly. For all that is spiritual and of lofty understanding is great.

04_marg1050: And seeing within it, etc. ISIDORE. Moses, that is, Christ, is found by the faithful at the river of washing and the water of baptism. 04_marg1051: And when he was grown up, she delivered, etc. RABANUS. Josephus relates that Pharao’s daughter brought Moses, grown up, to her father, who set his crown on him; which Moses at once threw down, because he saw an image carved on it. Hence the priest who was there wished to kill him, saying that Egypt was to be overthrown through him, as he had learned from an oracle of the demons. But Pharao’s daughter freed him. And when he was of full age, he was sent by Pharao against the Ethiopians. And since he knew that he would march through deserts full of serpents, he took ibises, that is, Egyptian storks. And when he had pitched camp, he brought them out, so that they might devour and drive off the serpents; and so the army passed the night safely. So when he came to the city he was to storm, the queen of the Ethiopians fell in love with him, and by agreement handed the city over to him and married him. Hence it is that Aaron and Mary quarrelled with Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife.

04_marg1052: AUGUSTINE. Of this deed of Moses we have argued enough in the work we wrote against Faustus on the life of the patriarchs: whether there was a praiseworthy disposition in him, by which he committed this sin, as rich ground is praised before useful seeds for a certain wildness of useless weeds; or whether the deed itself is to be justified. Which seems not to be so, because he did not yet hold any lawful power, neither received from God nor ordained by human society. 04_marg1067: I have seen the affliction, etc. GREGORY. Morally. When minds are scattered abroad it is hard for anyone to return to himself. For crooked ways, once they have caught a man, hold him the more delightfully, the more what he likes is not lawful. For when the gift of discipline does not stand in the way, no penalty of retribution is foreseen to frighten him. But with the eyes of the heart shut, the soul is hurled headlong, and the more securely it enters into temporal evils, the more stubbornly it despairs of eternal goods. But this wickedness of the reprobate separates the life of the elect, as grain from chaff, and while it afflicts, it profits them: because while it inflicts violence, it compels them to hasten to things above. This is signified in the people of Israel, with Moses calling and Pharao raging. For Moses was sent to call when Pharao pressed with hard works, so that one by calling might draw, another by raging might drive, so that the people, shamefully fixed in slavery, might be moved, either called or driven. This is done daily when, after the heavenly rewards are preached, the reprobate are allowed to rage against the elect: so that those whom Egypt, that is, the present life, oppressed by flattering, it may help by pressing; so that while God invites, torment may drive.

04_marg1075: GREGORY. Moses is the Jewish people; the rod, the power of the Godhead; the serpent, Christ’s mortality: for since death came through the serpent, mortality is signified by the serpent. Or because it is written, “Be ye wise as serpents,” and because the highest wisdom, that is, the Wisdom of God, was made flesh, his mortality is rightly figured in the serpent. Hence: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up.” Moses held the rod, because the Jewish people, before the Redeemer’s coming, trusted in the power of God. He casts it on the ground, because through the patriarchs and prophets it announced that God would be incarnate; the rod is turned into a serpent, because Christ, God remaining in himself, was made mortal in man. But Moses, seeing the serpent, was afraid and fled, because the Jewish people, when it saw Christ mortal, was afraid to believe him God. He is ordered to take hold of the tail, because the people that now refuses to believe will gather itself to the faith in the last part of the Lord’s body, that is, in the later time of the Church, namely at the end of the world; holding the serpent’s tail, because him whom it had before despised as mortal it will confess as its Redeemer in the last part of the Church. At once the serpent returns into a rod, because as soon as the Jewish people has believed in Christ, he will soon appear for judgment in the power of his Godhead, so that now the serpent is a rod: because he who on earth was despised as a man, coming from heaven, will be seen as God above the angels.

04_marg1078: I beseech thee, Lord, etc. AUGUSTINE. When Moses says to the Lord, “I pray, Lord, I am not eloquent before yesterday nor before the day before, nor since thou didst begin to speak to thy servant,” he is understood to believe that by God’s will he could suddenly be made eloquent, when he says “nor since thou didst begin to speak to thy servant”: as if showing that it could have happened that one who had not been eloquent before yesterday and the day before should suddenly become so from the time the Lord began to speak with him.
04_marg1079: Allegorically. While Moses was in Egypt and was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, he was not thin of voice, nor slow of tongue, nor did he profess himself ineloquent. For, as far as the Egyptians went, he was of a sonorous voice and of incomparable eloquence. But when he heard the voice of God and received the words of the Lord, he feels his voice thin and slight and slow, and his tongue hindered, and he declares himself dumb, when he begins to know the true Word, which was in the beginning with God. For though an untaught man be compared with dumb animals, he will seem eloquent; but compared with the learned and eloquent, foolish and dumb. But if anyone looks to the Word of God and the divine wisdom, he will profess himself a dumb animal before God far more than the cattle are before us. Hence: “I am become as a beast before thee.” So because he advanced so far in understanding as to know himself, which is a great part of wisdom, the divine favour rewards him, saying: “I will open thy mouth,” etc. Blessed are those whose mouth God opens, that they may speak. Hence: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.” Likewise Paul says: “That speech may be given me, that I may open my mouth.” So God opens the mouth of those who speak the words of God. The devil opens the mouth of those who speak lies, false witness, buffoonery, filthiness, and of whisperers and detractors, and of those who speak idle words. Of Judas it is related that Satan entered into him and put it into his heart to betray him. So he opened his mouth, that he might speak with the Pharisees how he should betray him for money received. And it is no small grace to tell apart the mouth that God opens and the one the devil opens. God also opens the ears of the saints to hear the divine words. Hence: “The Lord will open my ear”; he will open the eyes, as he “opened the eyes” of Agar, and she saw “a well of living water.” Hence Eliseus: “Open, Lord, the eyes of thy servant, that he may see, for there are more with us.” But the ear that is opened through the Lord’s instruction is sometimes open, sometimes shut. Hence: “Thou shalt not receive a vain report.” If vain, profane, filthy things are said, he who knows the Lord’s instruction shuts his ear and says: “But I, as a deaf man, heard not: and as a dumb man not opening his mouth.” But if what is said bears on the good of the soul, if the talk is of God, if it teaches morals, invites to virtues, cuts away vices, let the ears be open and the whole door of the soul. And note that the law used the greatest restraint in saying, “Thou shalt not receive a vain report.” It did not say “thou shalt not hear,” but “thou shalt not receive.” For we often hear vain things: Marcion and Valentius, and all who argue against the Creator, speak vain things; yet we often hear them, in order to answer them, but we do not receive them, because the devil opens their mouth. May the Lord deign to open our mouth, that we may be able to refute the gainsayer and stop the mouth that the devil opens.

04_marg1083: The Lord being angry at Moses, said, etc. AUGUSTINE. He seems not to have given him, as one distrustful, the fullest power he was going to give, and to have willed that what could have been done through one, had he believed, be done through two. But if you consider carefully, the Lord, being angry, does not seem to have given Aaron by way of punishment. For he says: “Is not Aaron the Levite thy brother? I know that he speaketh well.” In these words it is shown rather that he rebuked him because he feared to go, as if less fit, when he had a brother through whom he could speak what he wished to the people. For he was thin of voice and slower of tongue, though he ought to have hoped for everything from God. Indeed, even when angry he said what he had promised before. For he had said: “I will open thy mouth and instruct thee.” But now he says: “I will open thy mouth and his mouth, and will instruct you in what you shall do.” But because he added, “and he shall speak for thee to the people,” the opening of the mouth seems to have been granted because Moses said he was slower of tongue. But as to the thinness of his voice the Lord willed to grant him nothing, but for this he added the help of his brother, who with a fitting voice would be equal to teaching the people. And when he says, “And thou shalt put my words in his mouth,” he shows that he would give them by speaking. For if only by hearing, as he would speak into the ears of the people; then what he says after, “And he shall speak for thee to the people, and he shall be thy mouth,” here too “to the people” is understood. And when he says “he shall speak for thee to the people,” he points to the leadership in Moses, the ministry in Aaron. And as to his saying, “But thou shalt be to him in those things that pertain to God,” a great mystery is perhaps to be sought here: whose figure Moses bears, as a mean between God and Aaron, and Aaron between Moses and the people.

Another text has: “And it came to pass on the way at the resting place, an angel met him and sought to kill him; and Sephora, taking a pebble, circumcised the foreskin of her son, and fell at his feet and said: The blood of my infant’s circumcision has stopped. And he departed from him because she said: The blood of the circumcision has ceased.” First it is asked whom the angel wished to kill: whether Moses, because it is said, “An angel met him and sought to kill him”? For whom is he thought to have met, but him who was over them all? Or was he seeking to kill the boy, whom his mother helped by circumcising him, so that he is understood to have willed to kill the infant because he was not circumcised, in order to sanction the command of circumcision by this severity? If that is so, it is at first uncertain of whom he said, “He sought to kill him,” but it is made clear from what follows. It is indeed a wonderful and unusual expression, that he should say first, “He met him and sought to kill him,” of one of whom he had said nothing before. Like this is that: “The foundations thereof are in the holy mountains: the Lord loveth the gates,” etc. For “the foundations” can be understood as “of the Lord” or “of Sion,” because this pronoun “eius” is of every gender; but in Greek it is said autes in the feminine, autu in the masculine and neuter, and the Greek codex has autu, which compels us to understand not the foundations “of Sion” but “of the Lord.” But rather it is to be asked what it means that the angel withdrew from killing either of them because the woman said, “The blood of the infant’s circumcision has stopped.” For it does not say, “He departed from him because she circumcised the infant,” but because the blood of the circumcision stopped; not because it ran but because it stopped: a great mystery, unless I am mistaken.

Rightly is his mouth opened who meets him on the mountain of God: Peter, James and John on the mountain were found worthy to see the Lord Jesus transfigured, and Moses and Elias with him in glory. You too, unless you climb the mountain of God and meet Moses there, that is, unless you climb up to the lofty sense of the law, unless you take the summit of spiritual understanding, the door is not opened by the Lord. If you stand in the low place of the letter, you have not met Moses on the mountain of God; God has not opened your mouth, nor instructed you in what you ought to speak. Had Aaron not met Moses on the mountain, had he not seen his lofty sense, he would not have spoken to him the words of God nor handed on to him the power of the signs, nor made him a sharer in so great a mystery.

04_marg1092: Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice, etc. You see what raw pride does; you will see a little later how much it gains under the scourges, how much better he is made when beaten, who now says, “I know not the Lord,” and when beaten will say, “Pray the Lord for me.” So let no one be so untaught in the divine discipline as to think the divine scourges ruin and a penal death. See, even the hardest Pharao gains when beaten: for before the blows he does not know the Lord, and when beaten he asks that prayer be made for him, and gaining in the punishments, he knows how to recognize why he is punished. “I know not the Lord,” he says. In the Gospel, beaten, he amends this word, for the demons cried out: “We know who thou art. Thou art the Son of the living God.” After the scourges he will also let Israel go, and will even urge them to go out. It is asked how it is said to the people that God commanded that he would cast them out of Egypt into the land of Chanaan, while to Pharao it is said that they wished to go out a three days’ journey to sacrifice in the desert to their God at his command. But it is to be understood that, although God knew what he would do, since he foreknew that Pharao would not consent to let the people go, that was said first which would have happened first if he had let them go: for that all things should happen as the following Scripture bears witness, the stubbornness of Pharao and his people deserved. 04_marg1094: Morally. We set out a three days’ journey from Egypt if we so keep ourselves from all defilement of soul and body and spirit that our spirit, and soul, and body may be preserved whole unto the day of Christ.
04_marg1095: We set out a three days’ journey from Egypt if, taking rational, moral and natural wisdom away from worldly things, we turn it to the divine ordinances. We set out a three days’ journey from Egypt if, purifying in ourselves what is said, done or thought (for these are the three things through which men can sin), we are made clean of heart, so that we can see God. But the prince of Egypt, when he sees himself pressed harder to let the people of God go, seeks in the second place to obtain that they go no further, that they do not go the whole three days. Saying, “Go not far,” he does not want the people of God to be far from him. For he wants them to sin, if not in deed, then in word; if not in word, then in thought. He does not want them to go the whole three days from him. He wants to possess in us one day, in others two, in others the whole three days. Blessed are those who go away from him the whole three days.

04_marg1098: Now too Moses, whom we have with us (for we have Moses and the prophets), that is, the law of God, wishes to lead you out of Egypt, if you hear him; he wishes to put you far from Pharao, to rescue you from the work of clay and straw, if only you hear him and understand spiritually. 04_marg1099: Why do you Moses and Aaron, etc. ORIGEN. While the people is with him and works clay or brick, while it is busy with straw, he does not think it perverted, but going on rightly. But if it says, “I wish to go a three days’ journey and serve the Lord,” he says the people is being perverted by Moses and Aaron. Today too, if Moses and Aaron, that is, the word of prophet and priest, urge the soul to the service of God, to go out of the world, to renounce all that it possesses, to attend to the law and the word of God, at once you will hear the like-minded friends of Pharao saying: See how men are led astray and young men are perverted, so as not to work, not to serve as soldiers, not to do anything useful; leaving necessary things, they follow trifles and idleness. What is it to serve God? They do not want to work and they seek occasions for idleness. These were Pharao’s words then; these his friends speak now too, and they persecute not only with words but with blows. He orders the scribes of the Hebrews to be scourged, straw not to be given, the work to be exacted. Our fathers suffered these things, and now the people of God suffers them. Those who have given themselves wholly to the prince of this world prosper; all things, as they think, turn out happily. But for the servants of God not even a small and humble living succeeds. For these are the straws that were given by Pharao. Hence some, worn out, say to Pharao: “Why dost thou afflict thy people?” For overcome by blows they fall from the faith and confess that they are Pharao’s people. “For all are not Israelites that are of Israel.”

04_marg1102: The Lord see, etc. GREGORY. Morally. When the divine light enlightens the human heart, temptations soon grow up against it from the devil, so that it feels itself pressed by temptations more than when it did not know the rays of the inner light. Hence the Israelites, after they were called, complain against Moses about their growing labour, saying: “The Lord see and judge,” etc. For from those who wished to depart from Egypt Pharao had taken away the straw, and required work of the same measure. So the mind as it were murmurs against the law, after knowing which it bears sharper goads of temptation; and in that it displeases the adversary, seeing its labours grow, it grieves as if it stank in the eyes of Pharao.
04_marg1103: Because you have made … to stink, etc. ORIGEN. They speak the truth, though they do not know it; as Caiphas, who said, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people,” did not know what he was saying. For as the Apostle says, “We are the good odour of Christ, to some unto life, to others unto death,” so the prophetic word is a sweet savour to believers; but to the doubtful and unbelieving, and to those who confess themselves Pharao’s people, it becomes an accursed savour. Moses himself too says to the Lord: “Since I spoke with Pharao, thou hast afflicted thy people”; because before the word of God is heard, there is no tribulation or temptation; but when the trumpet of preaching has given the signal of war, the battle of tribulations arises. So from the time Moses and Aaron began to speak to Pharao, the people of God is afflicted. From the time the word of God was brought forth into your soul, a struggle of the virtues against the vices is stirred up within you, which before lasted in peace within you. But when the word of God began to make the division in each one, a great disturbance arises, and war is born without treaty, because injustice does not agree with justice, nor drunkenness with sobriety, nor a lie with the truth. So let us not be troubled if we seem an accursed savour to Pharao. For virtue is called the execration of vice. But as Moses stood before Pharao, let us too stand, let us not be bent, having our loins girt about with truth, and our feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace. And we stand confidently if we pray the Lord to set our feet upon a firm rock, lest our feet be moved. Let us stand, that is, resist, according to that: “Whom resist ye, strong in faith,” that Satan may soon be crushed under our feet. For the more steadily and bravely we stand, the weaker Pharao is. But if we begin to be weak or doubtful, he will become stronger. For when Moses lifted up his hands, Amalec was overcome; when he let them drop as if tired, he prevailed. So let us lift up our arms in the power of the cross of Christ, and raise holy hands in prayer, that we may deserve the help of God. Hence James says: “Resist the devil, and he will fly from you.” So let us act so that he not only flees but is crushed under our feet: so Pharao was destroyed in the depth of the abyss. And we, if we go back out of the Egypt of the vices, escape the waves of the world as though on a solid road, through Jesus Christ.

04_marg1115: Behold I have appointed thee God, etc. AUGUSTINE. Note that when he was sent to the people, it was not said to him, “Behold, I have given thee as a god to the people, and thy brother shall be thy prophet,” but, “Thy brother shall speak for thee to the people.” It was also said, “He shall be thy mouth, and thou to him in the things that are toward God”; it was not said, “Thou to him a god.” But to Pharao Moses is said to be given as a god; by analogy, Aaron is prophet to Moses, but toward Pharao. Here it is suggested to us that the prophets of God speak what they hear from him, and that a prophet of God is nothing other than one who announces the words of God to men who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God.
04_marg1116: Sometimes “God” is said in name, sometimes in essence. In name, as here: “I have appointed thee the God of Pharao.” And elsewhere: “Bring him to the gods.” And elsewhere: “God hath stood in the congregation of gods,” etc. In essence, as here: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Wishing to distinguish this, Paul says: “Of whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all things, God blessed for ever.” For one is called God in name among all things, but in essence above all things; so, to show that Christ is God by nature, he recorded that he is not only God, but God above all things. For any just man is a god, but among all things, because in name; but Christ above all things, because God by nature.

04_marg1117: But I shall harden his heart, etc. AUGUSTINE. God says constantly, “I will harden Pharao’s heart,” and brings in as it were the cause why he does this: “I will harden Pharao’s heart, and I will fulfil my signs and my wonders in Egypt,” as if Pharao’s hardening were needed for the signs to be multiplied or fulfilled. So God makes good use of evil hearts, for what he wishes to show to the good and what he will do for the good. And although the quality of each heart in its malice, that is, what kind of heart it has toward evil, comes about by its own fault, which has grown up from its free choice, yet that this evil quality should be moved this way or that, whether it is moved wickedly this way or that, comes about through causes by which the mind of man is driven on; and whether these exist or not is not in man’s power, but they come from the hidden providence of God, who justly and wisely orders and governs all that he created. So that Pharao had such a heart that the patience of God did not move him to piety but rather to impiety was his own fault; but that those things were done which his heart, so malignant by its own fault, resisted, the commands of God (for this is what is called hardened, because it did not consent pliably but resisted unbendingly), was of the divine dispensation, by which a plainly just penalty was prepared for such a heart, by which those who fear God might be corrected. For when a gain is set before them (for example) for which a murder might be committed, the greedy man is moved one way, the despiser of money another: the one to commit the crime, the other to beware of it. Yet the setting forth of the gain was not in their power. So causes come to the wicked which are not in their power, but they make of them what the causes find them already made by their own vices, of their own will. “I will harden” can also be taken thus: I will show how hard it is.

Here there was no need of the voice, for whose thinness Aaron seemed to have been given to Moses; but the rod was to be cast down to become a dragon. Why then did Moses not do this himself, unless because Aaron’s mediation between Moses and Pharao bears the figure of a great faith? 04_marg1123: The Apostle says: “Be zealous for the better gifts,” elsewhere, “for spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy.” Let us too try to take up the zeal for good things, and to wait for the fulness of the gift from the Lord. For to this it is said: “Open thy mouth, and I will fill it.” And to that: “He that pricketh the eye bringeth out tears: and he that pricketh the heart bringeth forth feeling.” I think, then, that Moses coming to Egypt and bearing the rod with which he chastises and strikes Egypt with ten plagues is the law of God, which reproves and amends the world with ten plagues, that is, with the ten commands of the decalogue. The rod by which these things are done, and Egypt subdued, and Pharao overcome, is the cross of Christ, through which the world and the prince of the world is overcome, that is, the devil with the principalities and powers. The rod cast down becomes a dragon or serpent and devours the serpents of the Egyptian magicians. Now the serpent is usually put for wisdom or prudence. Hence: “Be ye wise as serpents.” And elsewhere: “The serpent was more subtle than any of the beasts,” etc. So the cross of Christ, whose preaching seemed foolish, which Moses, that is, the Law, contains, according to that, “For he wrote of me,” after it was cast on the earth, that is, came to the faith of men, was turned into wisdom, and into such wisdom as would devour all the wisdom of the Egyptians, that is, of this world. For see how God made foolish the wisdom of this world, after he made known that Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God; and now the whole world is caught by him who said: “I will catch the wise in their own craftiness.”
04_interl2597: The preaching of the cross seemed foolish, but after it came to the faith of men, it is understood to be wisdom.
04_marg1124: ISIDORE. Moses cast down the rod before Pharao, and having become a serpent it devoured the serpents of the Egyptians, signifying that the Word would be made flesh, and would empty the serpents of their dire poison by the remission of sins. For the rod is the straight word, royal, full of power, the badge of rule. The rod became a serpent, since he who was the Son of God, born of God the Father, became the son of man, born of a virgin, who, lifted up on the cross like the serpent, poured healing into human wounds. Hence: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert,” etc. For the rod of Moses, turned into a dragon, swallowed up the rods of the magicians; and Christ, after the dignity of his glory, “became obedient unto death.” Through the very death of the flesh he consumed the sting of death, according to that: “O death, I will be thy death.”
04_marg1125: And it was turned, etc. The law of Moses was tasteless, as it were, like a rod; but turned into a serpent, that is, into spiritual understanding, it was made drinkable and delightful.
