04_interl4297: which is five taken four times; and there are five senses of the body, which he who enters the Church must subject to the divine commands.
04_interl4298: with the hope of heavenly things
04_interl4299: with the endurance of temporal things
04_interl4300: with the ardour of perfect charity
04_interl4301: and with continence of the flesh
04_interl4302: because the virtues themselves bestow mutual brightness on one another by kindred fellowship
04_marg1604: OF VIOLET etc. BEDE. Rightly in this entrance of the court the hanging is made, not as in the other court, of fine twisted linen, but of four most noble colours: namely violet and purple, and scarlet twice dyed, and fine twisted linen, with embroidered work; because to those who are catechized the face of the Church shines without, but its virtue will appear brighter and worthier to those who enter it through the sacraments of baptism. For no one becomes highest of a sudden, but by degrees we tend from lesser things to more perfect. Violet signifies the hope of heavenly goods; purple, the endurance of temporal evils; scarlet twice dyed, the ardour of perfect love; fine twisted linen, continence of the flesh. Which colours are diversified one with another in embroidered work, because each virtue of the faithful grows by the fellowship, as it were the kinship, of the virtues near it, although single colours could befit single elect persons. For he who gazes more loftily on heavenly things is violet; he who suffers more for justice' sake is purple; he who blazes with more fervent charity toward God and neighbour, scarlet twice dyed; he who spiritually grows white with virginal integrity of the flesh, fine twisted linen. And when the just, in the same faith and gospel piety, rejoice together in one another's virtues, it is as if a hanging, woven with fair variety of colours, adorned the entrance of the Lord's court.
04_interl4303: because they who enter the Church must order their faith and action according to the rule of the Gospels
04_marg1605: AND IT SHALL HAVE FOUR PILLARS etc. BEDE. In the entrance of the court there are four pillars, because we enter the unity of the Church only through the faith and sacraments of the Gospel, which are contained in four books. Whence the beginnings of the four Gospels are recited to those to be catechized, and they are skilfully instructed concerning their figures and order at the opening of the ears, that they may know thenceforth and remember which and how many are the books by whose words they must chiefly be instructed in the faith of the Trinity. In which entrance a hanging of twenty cubits is made, which is four taken five times. And there are five senses of the body. Well therefore at the entrance of the court is a hanging of twenty cubits hung on four pillars, because all who enter the Church must order their faith and their acts alike according to the rule of the Gospels, that, holding back from the allurements of the flesh, they may subject the senses of the body to the divine commands. For not only is this hanging raised on four pillars, but it also has in its length the number five multiplied, when any humble and pious hearers coming to the faith, desiring not only to be imbued with the words of the Gospel but also to lead the gospel life, spend all the senses of the body in the obedience of charity.
04_interl4306: with the observance and proclaiming of the divine words
04_interl4307: "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire" etc.
04_interl4309: because they must subject themselves to the divine precepts as to a silver head
04_interl4310: who must apply themselves in body and mind to the labour of preaching
04_interl4311: because they are to be established in the fear of the Lord
04_interl4312: because it lifts up its arms to good works for the sake of eternal unity
04_marg1606: ALL THE PILLARS etc. BEDE. He presses home more carefully what he had said, that he may earnestly admonish the reader that no one can be counted among the doctors of truth, namely the pillars of the heavenly court, who has not learned to have, like brass, an unconquerable patience amid adversities; unless he has adorned himself, fortifying himself on every side with the observance and proclaiming of heavenly words as with plates of silver; unless he has put himself under the divine precepts with all subjection, as under a silver head, and established himself in the fear of God as on a brazen socket.
04_interl4314: because it hopes for rest in the grace of the Holy Ghost
04_interl4315: because of the five senses of the body, because in the body we shall receive what we have done in the body
04_interl4316: with chaste heart, namely, and work
04_interl4317: fixed, namely, in the fear of God
04_marg1607: IN LENGTH etc. BEDE. The Church has a hundred cubits of length, which lifts up its arms to good works for the sake of eternal life. Fifty of breadth, because it hopes for everlasting rest in the grace of the Holy Ghost, which he willed to be signified by the number fifty, when he consecrated Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day of the Paschal feast, by his coming. The height is five cubits, according to the number of the senses of the body, because then every one shall receive the proper things of his body, according as he hath done, whether it be good or evil. But in the court of the house of God the figure of those only is expressed who have done good in the body, for which they deserve to be brought into the rest of everlasting life: who now shine like fine twisted linen in the works of justice which they do with chaste body and heart, and then in the same body, raised to the glory of immortality, the rewards of justice received. In the Gospel, however, mention is made of both parts, where five virgins with the works of light at once go in with the bridegroom to the marriage; but five, who had done the works of chastity with no chaste mind, are shut out with their darkness. For there were five, and five, both of whom were judged according to the things they had done in the flesh. The whole length and breadth of the court therefore is marked out by a hundred and fifty cubits. It has five cubits of height, because it is necessary that we who have the promise of rest and the heavenly fatherland cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit, and perfect sanctification in the fear of God, that when the hour of the promised reward appears we may rejoice in spirit and flesh in the love of God, because of the cleansing of both our substances, that is, of soul and flesh, in the fear of God. What had been said above is repeated also, that it may be the more firmly committed to memory: And it shall be made of fine twisted linen etc.
04_interl4318: the saints, serving with divers merits and degrees
04_interl4320: the tongues of the preachers, which by preaching touch the hearts of the hearers, and by touching lift them up
04_interl4321: that they may remember to persevere amid adversities and to sound forth the faith
04_marg1608: ALL THE VESSELS etc. BEDE. These vessels are the men in the Church who serve the Lord with divers merits and degrees, which are commanded to be made of brass, that each may persevere to the end in adversities, lest he lose by sloth the salvation promised him; or that he may not fear to confess openly to assailing enemies the faith he has learned, and may not cease to sound forth to friends the gifts he has received. For brass is sounding and lasting. And the pins of the tabernacle or the court were made for this, that, fixed in the tops of the pillars, they might stand out on the outside, and, the cords of the veils or hangings being laid on them, might so raise them and hold them up from the ground. By their making and placing the tongue of the doctors is signified, which by preaching touches the hearts of the hearers, and by touching lifts them up. For Scripture is wont to be signified by cords. Whence: "A threefold cord is not easily broken", because Scripture, which is wont to be interpreted in the historical and allegorical or moral sense, is corrupted by no perversity of heretics or pagans. And the hangings or veils, that they might receive the cords, had in their upper parts loops or rings into which the cords might be put. Thou also, if thou wilt become a hanging of God, prepare in thy heart a receptacle for the word, that thou mayest be lifted up to things above; and let the cords of the hangings be laid on the pins of the pillars, that so spread out and raised on high they may complete the beauty of the tabernacle. Let the preachers commit the divine words to the hearts of the faithful, by which they may raise them from the lowest things after their own example, that the veils or hangings, stretched by cords and lifted up, may show far and wide the wonderful beauty of their work, which, rolled up, they could not; let the faithful show the amplitude of good work, the beauty of mind and of inner grace, that others seeing may glorify the Father who is in heaven, saying: How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord.
04_interl4327: because in the Church the light of preaching ought never to be lacking, or the pure humility of hearers who gladly receive the word of God
04_interl4328: the works of the just, which shine as an example to others; whence: So let your light shine before men etc.
04_interl4330: Because within heaven there is no need of the lamp of the Scriptures, where is the ark of the Lord, and the cherubims of glory overshadow the propitiatory, that is, the hosts of the heavenly army praise with harmonious voice the glory of the incarnate Son, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation for our sins.
04_interl4332: no other, but those who shine with chastity of faith and the performance of work, as true priests of Christ
04_interl4333: because when the night of this world is past, the morning of the world to come will shine, of which it is said: "In the morning I will stand before thee, and will see" etc. In which the lamp of books will not be needed, the true light of the world appearing and enlightening, because unto them that fear the name of the Lord the sun of justice shall arise.
04_marg1609: COMMAND THE CHILDREN etc. BEDE. All the adornment of the tabernacle being set in order, the light of the lamp is next provided for, that its wonderful beauty, as by day with the light of the sun, so by night might be lit up by the flames of lamps; lest there ever be darkness or shadow in the house of God. Mystically, in the house of God the lamp is the works of the just, which enlighten the minds of those who behold them by their examples. But it is to be considered more carefully that, that a lamp might always burn in the tabernacle of God, the children of Israel are bidden to offer oil, but Aaron and his sons to order the lamp: because the faithful and beloved hearers bring hearts ready to obey the faith; but the doctors by preaching minister the fire of the heavenly word, by which they may be enlightened to know and inflamed to love God. For by the fatness of oil, by which the weary and the sick are refreshed and the grace of light is supplied, the inner love of the mind and the work of mercy are designated. Whence: But I, as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God etc.; as if to say: because I showed the fruit of mercy to the needy, I hoped that the grace of mercy would also be repaid to me by God for ever. Let the children of Israel therefore offer oil, but Aaron and his sons, fire being brought, order the lamp that is to burn in the tabernacle of God: the hearers, namely, the devotion of the mind, and let the doctors teach them the secrets of heavenly knowledge, instructed by which they may burn with the fire of charity in the sight of God, and show to men the light of good action.
04_marg1610: OF THE OLIVES etc. BEDE. It is to be noted that the children of Israel are bidden to offer oil, but with the distinction, of the olives, and there is added: the purest, and beaten with a pestle. For oil is wont to be made of myrtle, of radish, of nut, of wood, and of divers kinds; but none may be offered in the tabernacle of the Lord except that which is made of olives: as neither may any other fire than that which came down from heaven either burn in the lamps or be kindled on the altar of God: "For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful." Let the children of Israel therefore offer oil for the lamps of God, not any whatever, but of olives, the purest, and beaten with a pestle. Let the hearers offer to the doctors a pure conscience, fruitful with the grace of charity, cleansed by the pestle of diligent proving from all mixture of wickedness, which delights to hear the words with the sole intention of pleasing and serving God. Let Aaron with his sons offer not strange fire, but that sent from above, and for kindling the lamp, as for consuming the holocausts and burning the incense, let the doctors preach the word, not their own, but the Lord's, according to that: For we are not as many, adulterating the word of God etc. Let them use this fire to light up the knowledge of the faith, the hearts of the hearers for completing and consecrating the holocausts of their works, for kindling the incense of prayers.
04_marg1611: AND AARON SHALL ORDER etc. BEDE. For it is not for all to preach the sacraments of faith to the people, but only for those who by chastity of faith and exercise of work are proved to belong to the sons of the high priest of God. For he who strays from purity of faith by wicked doctrine, or stains the integrity of faith by wickedness of works, even if he stands out in the name or person of a priest, let him hear from the Lord: "Why dost thou declare my justices" etc.? To such James says: "Be ye not many masters, my brethren" etc.
04_interl4334: in the Church, not in the tabernacle
04_marg1612: IT SHALL BE A PERPETUAL OBSERVANCE etc. BEDE. This clause, like the things that concern the tabernacle, its vessels and utensils, is to be understood and expounded spiritually, not carnally. For how will the worship of the priestly office be perpetual, when the priesthood itself, and the tabernacle in which it was carried on, and the people for whom it was carried on, have long since ceased? In holy Church therefore this is fulfilled, where, the doctors succeeding one another in order, with the hearers of the truth, there will never be lacking spiritual children of Israel to offer gifts of piety in the house of the Lord, and sons of Aaron, that is, our true priests, to bestow on them the light of the word, until, the state of this world being fulfilled, and the whole tabernacle, that is, the multitude of the elect, being carried over to heaven, there be no longer men to be taught by men, since "God shall be all in all".
04_interl4337: Moses signifies the Law, Aaron the priests, whom the Law takes to itself, because the priests ought always to continue in the meditation of the Law.
04_interl4339: by grace; to the law: the New Testament must be joined to the Old
04_interl4340: the doctors ought so to study the divine law that they may be seen to be joined to it by kinship as brothers
04_interl4342: that they may excel the other elect
04_interl4343: in most copies is added: Eleazar and Ithamar
04_marg1613: TAKE UNTO THEE ALSO AARON THY BROTHER etc. BEDE. As the tabernacle with its adornments and vessels signifies the Church, distinguished by a fair variety of virtues and persons, so the high priest of the tabernacle signifies Christ the true high priest, who offered himself for us. Who is well called brother, because by a brotherly covenant, grace to the law, the New Testament is joined to the Old, since Moses himself says of him: The Lord will raise up to you a prophet of your brethren, like unto me. And a little after, in the person of the Lord: "I will raise them up a prophet out of the midst of their brethren like to thee"; to whose wonderful works, which no one else did, the habit of Aaron, remarkable for its wonderful variety, is compared. Or the manifold vestments of Aaron signify the whole company of the elect cleaving to Christ with a wonderful diversity of works and merits. Whence: As many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ. The sons of Aaron, joined in the priesthood, figure the apostles of Christ and all the masters of the Church.
04_marg1614: Take unto thee also Aaron thy brother etc. The making of the tabernacle having been described, the priests who are to minister in it are fittingly ordained. Whose ordination and habit befit the priests of the Church, so that all that shone bright outwardly there in the adornment of the vestments may, understood spiritually, stand out inwardly in the minds of our priests also, and shine glorious in their acts above the rest. Therefore Moses is commanded to take to himself his brother Aaron with his sons from among the children of Israel, to perform the priesthood before the Lord. For it is necessary that they who are to be promoted to a higher degree apply themselves with greater industry of mind to the law of God, that is, to the observance of the divine commandments. For this is what it is for those who are to perform the priesthood to be taken to Moses from among the children of God: for the prelates and doctors of the Church to pass beyond the common life of the elect by a singular height of mind, and to attend with intimate inspection to what the law speaks generally to the perfect, that by a loftier excellence of merits they may come to loftier rewards. Moses is commanded to ordain his brother with his sons to the priesthood, because all who are allotted the office of doctor ought to cleave to the law with such zeal and love that they may be seen to be joined to it by kinship as brothers. The first of the sons of Aaron, after their ordination, offering strange fire, perished by heavenly fire, because some, set in the place of priests, while they put the fire of covetousness before the fire of love from above, are consumed by the fire of vengeance from above.

04_interl4346: to the prophets, apostles and other doctors of truth, who teach by word and deed how the ministers of the altar should live

04_interl4348: "Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, coming down" etc.
04_marg1615: AND THOU SHALT MAKE A HOLY VESTURE etc. BEDE. The holy vestments of Aaron which Moses made for him are the works of justice and holiness which the Scripture of the sacred law commends to rulers to be had, whose examples to be imitated it shows in Christ. The wise of heart, whom God filled with the spirit of wisdom for making the vestments, are the prophets and apostles and the other doctors, who show by deed and word how priests ought to live and to minister at the altar: A bishop must be without crime, and a dispenser of the word of God.
04_interl4350: of the breast, which in Greek is logion
04_interl4351: of the shoulders, which in Hebrew is ephod
04_interl4352: the shirt which was put on underneath
04_interl4353: these two cover the whole body
04_interl4357: which binds both tunics and the ephod to the body
04_interl4358: they ought not to minister otherwise
04_interl4359: Nothing vile or base ought to be in the mouth or work of the priest.
04_marg1616: THESE ARE THE VESTMENTS etc. How each of these was made is set out more fully in what follows. The rational is a garment of the breast. The ephod is the tunic of the shoulders. And the strait linen garment, that is, the shirt, covers the whole body. The mitre adorns the head. The girdle fits both tunics together and the ephod more closely to the body. To these six garments a seventh is joined below; an eighth, namely the linen breeches, to cover the nakedness; and the golden plate upon the mitre, which with the title of the name of the Lord stood out higher than all. The strait linen garment clung to the body, so tight, with the sleeves drawn close, that there was no wrinkle in it, coming down to the legs. Whence in Greek it is called poderis, that is, reaching to the ankles. With these eight kinds of vestments the high priest was clothed at the time of sacrifice, four of which were allowed to the lesser priests, namely the breeches, the linen tunic, the girdle and the mitre. For it is fitting that he who is of greater grace and degree should shine admirable with more acts of virtue. And all are of gold and precious colours, because nothing vile and base ought to appear in the mouth or work of the priest, but all that he does, speaks and thinks ought to be illustrious before men and glorious in the sight of the inner judge.
04_marg1617: The priest is commanded to be bound on both shoulders with the covering of the ephod, that against adversity and prosperity he may always be fortified with the adornment of the virtues: that walking "by the armour of justice on the right hand and on the left", while he strives toward inner things alone, he may be bent to no side of low delight; that prosperity may not lift him up, nor adversity trouble him, nor flatteries soothe him to pleasure, nor harsh things press him into despair; that while he humbles the intention of his mind in those passions, he may show with how great beauty of the ephod he is covered on both shoulders. Which is made of gold, violet, purple, and scarlet twice dyed, and fine twisted linen, that it may be shown with how great a diversity of virtues he ought to shine. In the gold the understanding of wisdom is shown; to which violet is added, that what he understands may rise not to low favour but to the love of heavenly things, lest while he is taken with praises he be emptied of the understanding of truth. With these purple is mingled, that the priest's heart, while it hopes for the highest things it preaches, may also repress vices in itself with kingly power, beholding the nobility of the inner regeneration, and guarding for itself by its manners the entrance of the heavenly kingdom. Whence: You are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation. For of the power by which we subdue vices John says: "He gave them power to be made the sons of God." And David: "Their principality is exceedingly strengthened." To these the scarlet twice dyed is joined, that before the eyes of God all the goods of the virtues may be adorned from charity, and that the things that glow before men may be kindled with the flame of inner love. For charity, while it loves God and neighbour, shines as with a double dye. But when the mind is stretched out to the precepts of charity, it remains that the flesh be macerated by abstinence. Whence to the scarlet twice dyed twisted fine linen is added, which signifies the shining chastity of bodily cleanness; which, being twisted, is woven into the beauty of the ephod, because chastity is brought to the perfect whiteness of cleanness when the flesh is wearied by abstinence. And when among the other virtues the merit of afflicted flesh also advances, the twisted fine linen shines white as it were in the varied beauty of the ephod.
04_interl4360: first, namely, because the works of him who is promoted to the office of priest ought first to be known
04_interl4361: This ephod is said to have been in the manner of a cowl without sleeves, having a round cap and a square opening on the breast where the rational was placed.
04_interl4362: the labours of works, which the priest ought continually to present before the Lord
04_interl4363: that he may shine with the understanding of wisdom
04_interl4364: that through what he understands he may rise to the love of heavenly things
04_interl4365: that he may oppose vices with kingly power
04_interl4366: that he may love God and neighbour together
04_interl4367: with the whiteness of bodily cleanness
04_interl4370: with variety of virtues and works
04_marg1618: AND THEY SHALL MAKE etc. BEDE. Because we carry burdens on the shoulders, the ephod of the high priest shows the labours of good works, which he ought continually to bear before the Lord; which is well commanded to be made first. For let the works of those who are promoted to the priesthood and the mastership of God's people first be known, that when what lies open to all outwardly has been shown to be irreproachable, the integrity of the heart and the sincerity of faith may be proved. The ephod therefore signifies the gospel burden, of which it is said: "For my yoke is sweet and my burden light." And elsewhere: If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. And the ephod is made of gold, violet and purple, fine twisted linen, and scarlet twice dyed. Of gold, namely, that before all things in the priestly habit the understanding of wisdom may chiefly shine forth. To which the airy violet is joined, that what he penetrates by understanding may rise not to low favour but to the love of heavenly things, lest while he feeds on his own praises he be deprived of the understanding of truth. With the gold and violet purple also is mingled, that the priest's heart, while it hopes for the highest things it preaches, may in itself repress the suggestions of vices, and oppose them with kingly power, and guard by its manners the entrance of the heavenly kingdom. In the purple colour, however, the shedding of blood for Christ, or the endurance of divers pressures, can be understood. For this is the cross which we carry after the Lord. Such a beauty therefore shines on the shoulder of the priest as may teach him to be ready to suffer. And to the gold, violet and purple the scarlet twice dyed is joined, that before the eyes of the inner judge all the goods of the virtues may be adorned from charity; that the things that glow before men the flame of inner love may kindle in the sight of God; which charity, namely, by which he loves God and neighbour, shines as from a double dye. But when the mind is enlarged to the precepts of charity, it remains that the flesh be macerated by abstinence. Whence to the scarlet twice dyed twisted fine linen is joined, that is, the chastity of bodily cleanness, which, being twisted, is woven into the beauty of the ephod, because chastity is brought to the perfect whiteness of cleanness when the flesh is wearied by abstinence.
04_marg1619: AND SCARLET TWICE DYED etc. BEDE. Scarlet shines with the appearance of fire, and perhaps it is commanded to be made twice dyed because fire has a double power, namely of burning and of shining; whose nature the prelate of saving doctrine must imitate, that he may open the light of knowledge to those who desire it, and by rebuking burn up the rust of sins in the despisers. For when he sets out to his hearers the sweet secrets of the Scriptures, the miracles and the gospel parables, he shows as it were in his habit the brightness of light. But when, recalling the eternal vengeance, he smites the proud, he shows as it were the terror of devouring flame. For he who makes a sermon to the people ought to press neither on rebuking faults alone nor on unlocking the secrets of the Scriptures alone, lest, disputing only of the correction of sins, he be heard the less, or, unlocking only the secrets of the mysteries, he profit the less. Let him therefore temper his sermon from both, that he may lay open the sweetness of heavenly secrets and the correction of manners, showing as it were the scarlet twice dyed in his habit.
04_interl4373: that they may serve God in concord
04_marg1620: THE TWO EDGES etc. BEDE. Of this it is said in what follows: He made therefore the ephod of gold, violet and purple. And a little after: Two edges also coupled one to another on both sides from top to bottom, so that half of the garment appeared outside to the eyes of beholders, and the other half lay hid within, but both edges, joined together, went down to the lower parts as far as the extreme corners. In which it is understood typically that when we extend good works outwardly to our neighbours, we should keep them whole within before the Lord, lest a lesser perfection of action follow the chastity of pure thought, or a more imperfect intention of mind the perfection of action; but that, as the two edges of the ephod, they may be joined within by a pure and simple intention on both sides of the ephod, that amid adversity and prosperity we may serve the Lord with concordant action. For an edge falls short, as the shorter of the wider, and with discordant measure they cannot come back into one, if, while we are seen outwardly to do good for an eternal reward, we are entangled in the secret of the mind with the intention of pleasing men, and seek the rewards of human favour rather than of the invisible life.
04_marg1621: BEDE. The gold was not in one part, the violet or other colours in another, but all were woven together with the gold throughout, because in the action of the priest none of the great virtues ought to be left off even for an hour; but to the gold of wisdom let there be joined, raised on high by the violet of hope, and great-souled against the wars of vices by the purple of the heavenly kingdom; the priest ought always to be bright with the scarlet twice dyed of twofold love, and with the twisted fine linen, that is, of chastened flesh.
04_interl4374: because the works of the saints ought to be turned over in a precious and clean heart
04_marg1622: TWO STONES etc. That the priest may imitate the faith and life of the patriarchs, and be mindful of the twelve tribes in sacrifices and prayers, and that the people, beholding, may not stray from the merits of the patriarchs.
04_interl4375: The precious stones are the works of the virtues.
04_interl4376: because every action and intention of the high priest ought to be fenced about with the cleanness and brightness of wisdom
04_interl4377: with the understanding of wisdom and with charity
04_marg1623: SET IN GOLD etc. BEDE. Fittingly are the stones commanded to be set in gold and compassed about: for by gold understanding or charity is intimated, because as gold excels metals, so charity excels the other virtues. And the precious stones are set and compassed about with gold when the working of the virtues is looked round on every side with pure understanding, that no vice may be allowed to lie hid, no filth to remain, and the virtues themselves are so held by the bond of charity that by no changeableness of things can they fall from their state, or slip from the habit of the priest through a sluggish watch of the mind.
04_interl4378: that, seeing, they may be mindful of the fathers
04_interl4379: that, namely, he may imitate the deeds and examples of those whose names he bears, and be mindful of them in the sacred prayers
04_marg1624: Because the priest, carefully weighing at every hour the life of the saints who went before, ought to be fortified with the adornment of the virtues in adversity and prosperity, that walking "by the armour of justice on the right hand and on the left" he may be bent to no side of low delight.
04_marg1625: For three reasons Aaron always bore the names of the patriarchs on his shoulders, as also on his breast, during the sacrifices: that he himself, namely, might remember to imitate the faith and life of the patriarchs; that he might be mindful in prayers and sacrifices of the twelve tribes which were born of them; that the people, seeing the names of the fathers written on the vesture of the prelate, might take earnest care not to depart from their merits and turn aside to the contagion of errors. Whence: And thou shalt put them in both sides of the ephod, a memorial for the children of Israel. Now also the high priest bears the names of the patriarchs on the ephod when the doctor or prelate of the Church considers in all he does the deeds of the fathers who went before, and strives to direct his life to their imitation, and to bear the burden of gospel perfection. And well are the names of the fathers graven in precious stones. The precious stones are the works of the spiritual virtues. And the priest has precious stones on his shoulders, and the names of the fathers written on them, when he has stood forth admirable to all by the brightness of good works, and has taught that this same brightness was not newly found by himself but handed down to him by the ancient authority of the fathers. And he bears these on his shoulders for a twofold reason: that he himself may walk humbly subject to the precepts of the Lord, and may always set before his hearers heavenly examples, whether his own or the fathers', for them to follow.
04_marg1626: THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO HOOKS etc. BEDE. These hooks were skilfully fixed in the uppermost corners of the ephod; but the little chains seem to have been fastened, not on the ephod, but on the rational, that is, on its upper corners, through golden rings, so that when the high priest put it on, the chains which hung from the rational could also be fastened to the hooks of the ephod, that both might hold together in a firm position. Whence more plainly in what follows: They made on the rational little chains linked one to another of the purest gold, and two hooks, and as many rings of gold. And they put the rings on either side of the rational, from which hung two chains of gold, which they put into the hooks that stood out in the corners of the ephod. Of their figure it will be better treated in the exposition of the rational.
04_marg1627: These were on the edges of the ephod, by which the chains of the rational were joined to the ephod, because good works and clean thought are to be bound to one another through charity and good intention.
04_interl4381: in which is expressed the chastity of the heart and thoughts of the priest, whose breast is covered and adorned by the rational
04_interl4382: that he may do all things with discretion
04_marg1628: THE RATIONAL ALSO etc. GREGORY. It is commanded that the rational of judgment be fastened on the breast of Aaron with binding fillets, lest loose thoughts possess the priestly heart, but reason alone constrain it, lest he think anything indiscreet or useless who, set up as an example, ought always to show by the gravity of his life how much reason he bears in his breast. On the rational the twelve names of the patriarchs are described: to bear the fathers written always on the breast is to think on the life of the ancients without ceasing. For then the priest walks irreproachably, when, always beholding the examples of the fathers who went before, he presses down unlawful thoughts, lest he set his foot outside the bound of order. It is called the rational of judgment because the ruler ought with subtle examination to discern good and evil, and to think diligently what things befit whom, when and how, to seek nothing of his own, but to count the good of his neighbours his own advantage. Whence: "And thou shalt put in the rational of judgment doctrine and truth" etc. For the priest bears the judgment of the children of Israel on his breast in the sight of the Lord when he examines the causes of those subject to him with regard to the inner judge alone, that he mingle nothing human in what he dispenses set in God's stead, lest private grief embitter correction. And when he shows himself zealous against the vices of others, let him carry out what is his own, lest either hidden envy stain the tranquillity of judgment or headlong anger disturb it. But while the terror of him who presides over all, that is, of the inner judge, is considered, let the subjects be ruled not without great fear.
04_marg1629: The rational also etc. As in the ephod the perfection of works, so in the rational of judgment, by which the breast of the priest is covered and adorned, the chastity of his heart and thoughts is expressed. And well does the rational of judgment follow the ephod, that when one has appeared before men innocent in hands, he may strive much more to stand clean in heart in the sight of the highest judge, doing all things of set purpose, that whatever he does or judges outwardly toward his neighbours may shine as proved by the rule of inner reason and pleasing to his Maker. Again the priest is commanded to bear the rational of judgment on his breast, because the ruler ought with subtle examination to discern good and evil, and to think diligently what things befit whom, when or how.
04_interl4385: because thought ought to agree with work
04_interl4389: because on each side it had the measure of a span
04_interl4390: that it may strongly bear the weight of the gems
04_interl4391: that the examination of the priest may please God, and man not despise it
04_interl4392: the unwearied effort of pious intention
04_interl4393: of eternal life to be desired
04_interl4394: by the grace of charity toward the care of the neighbour
04_marg1630: BEDE. The rational was made so, that it might the more easily bear the weight of the stones. But typically it admonishes us that the invisible judge should approve the reason of our examination, and that human esteem without should not with cause despise it; or we bear a double rational of judgment on the breast when the things we speak or think of the faith of truth and the invisible life stand on fixed reason, and the things we do visibly or purpose to do are weighed by the judgment of discretion. And that it had the measure of a span every way shows the unwearied and perpetual effort of pious intention. For he who measures something with the span shows his hand with the fingers spread with utmost effort, that he may hold fully and surely the measure he seeks. Whence as by the hand working, so by the span the unbending intention of working is expressed; and well does the same rational have the measure of a span both in length and in breadth, because whether it raise the desire of the mind to the length of eternal life, or bend its affection in the breadth of charity to the care of the neighbour, it is necessary that the priestly heart be in no way slothful, but be stretched out with burning desire, that it may lay hold on "the prize of the supernal vocation of God".
04_interl4395: the setting of divers gems: the manifold grace of the virtues, which ought to appear in harmonious order in the heart of the priest
04_marg1631: AND THOU SHALT SET IN IT etc. BEDE. This setting of divers gems in the rational shows the manifold grace of various virtues, which ought to appear in harmonious order in the heart of the priest. And the single stones are inscribed with the single names of the fathers, when the ruler, looking into the life of the saints, searches carefully who flourished most in which works of the virtues, and gathers all these in the secret of his breast, and brings them forth by working. For by a great sacrament each vesture is crowned with precious stones and marked with the illustrious names of the fathers. And the same names on the ephod are graven on two stones of the same kind, but on the rational on twelve of different kind. That the fathers were graven on most precious stones, and not of different colour, signifies that one faith in God, and one charity, and hope of the heavenly life, filled the hearts of all the fathers. That they were written on stones of different kind is the manifold variety and grace of good works, by which the faith, hope and charity of the saints, confirmed, shine forth.
04_marg1632: In the rational there were four rows of stones, and each had three stones, that namely by the four principal virtues we may hold the unfeigned faith of the Trinity. For the priest has four rows of gems on his breast when all that he thinks has been circumspect with prudence, firm with fortitude, excellent with justice, separated from all evils by temperance. But the same rows have three gems each, when prudence, fortitude, justice and temperance stand in the faith and working of the Trinity. Fittingly therefore the priest, that he may shine in work, carries four rows of gems on his breast; and that with his works he may be chaste in sincerity of faith, he has three gems in each row, that he may show to all the confession of true faith and an action to be imitated, that they too may deserve to be made members of the high priest.
04_marg1633: We can indeed take in the varied beauty of the stones not only the manifold brightness of priestly action and knowledge, but also the gifts of spiritual virtues and the miracles of healing. Of which it is said: "Heal the sick" etc. And elsewhere: "And these signs shall follow them that believe: In my name they shall cast out devils." But whatever they designate, rightly is the number twelve commanded to be made in the rational, that we may know that the acts and miracles of those who follow the virtue of apostolic faith and charity are also acceptable to God. But if anyone speak with the tongues of angels, and distribute his goods to the poor, and deliver his body to be burned, if he have not the unity of catholic charity, it profits him nothing.
04_interl4396: in the four rows there are only three stones each, that is, in the principal virtues the faith of the Trinity
04_interl4397: which, as they say, like red earth, is commonly called cornelian
04_interl4398: the topaz, most precious, of all colours, and chiefly of gold; whence it is called topasion as it were topadion, that is, of all colours
04_interl4400: which is said to shine by night, and to light up all things around it
04_interl4402: of a dull green, which is said to give help against phantoms

04_interl4404: from the Achates, a river of Sicily, where it is found; and it is said to be of black colour, having white veins on its surface
04_interl4407: onyx in Greek, nail in Latin; whence the onyx is the stone which has the colour of a human nail
04_marg1634: BEDE. Rightly were two onyx stones on the ephod engraved with the same number of fathers, that they might designate that the doctrine and faith of the apostles would profit both peoples, namely of the Jews and of the gentiles. The onyx, of red colour, having circles with white girding bands, signifies the ardour of charity or the light of knowledge, with the band of chastity accompanying. The priest bears the names of the fathers inscribed on stones of this kind when he gives continual zeal to the charity, chastity, humility, doctrine and the other works of virtue of the just who went before, which are to be imitated; and this among both peoples, that Jew and gentile may behold in the doctor the brightness of truth and piety, through which he himself may advance to better things.
04_interl4408: of watery colour, which, as they say, cannot be engraved
04_interl4409: that the priest, looking at the life of the saints, with what virtues they flourished, may meditate and imitate by working
04_interl4410: which signifies the cleanness of thoughts
04_interl4411: the industry of mind which joins the understanding of the doctors with working, that they cannot be separated
04_interl4412: the continual remembrance of perpetual brightness in heaven
04_interl4414: the love of God and neighbour
04_interl4415: of the firm intention, namely, of pleasing God, which is wholly fit for receiving the love of God and neighbour, whether in prosperity or in adversity

04_interl4420: ingeniously or skilfully: for any craftsman is called faber.
04_marg1635: THOU SHALT MAKE ON THE RATIONAL etc. BEDE. The order of the work, so far as it seems to us, was this. There were two hooks set above in the two corners of the ephod, and two rings over against them in the two upper corners of the rational, from which hung two golden chains, which at the time of vesting were put into the hooks that stood out in the corners of the ephod, as is written more plainly in what follows, that the ephod and the rational might be bound to each other; whose upper joining has been described thus far. Then follows the lower, which was beneath the armpits, Scripture adding thus: Thou shalt make also two rings of gold, which thou shalt put in the top parts of the rational, in the borders that are over against the ephod, and look towards the back parts thereof. When it says, in the borders that are over against the ephod, it does not mean in the borders of the ephod, but in those borders which are over against the ephod, that is, in the borders of the rational which are over against the ephod. For the rings which were in the last and lowest corners of the rational had over against them on each side of the ephod likewise other rings, to which they were joined by binding fillets. Of which it follows: Moreover also other two rings of gold, which are to be set on each side of the ephod beneath, that looketh towards the nether joining, that the rational may be fitted with the ephod; because he had spoken before of the upper joining, which was above the shoulders. Between which joinings this was the difference, that the upper was made with little chains, the lower with binding fillets. Whence is added: "And the rational may be fastened by the rings thereof unto the rings of the ephod with a violet fillet, that the joining artificially wrought may continue, and the rational and the ephod may not be loosed one from the other." But it is not to be thought that both garments ended together. For the rational, which had the measure of a span in height and breadth, covered not much more than the breast. But the ephod reached to the girdle, as is plainly shown in what follows, when it is said: These answered so to one another before and behind, that the ephod and the rational were bound together, fastened to the girdle and coupled more firmly with rings, which a violet fillet joined, lest they should hang loose and be moved from one another.
04_marg1636: Allegorically. The ephod signifies the completion of good works, the rational the cleanness of thoughts. And the connexion, the industry of mind by which the understanding and faith of the doctors is joined with working. For the joining artificially wrought continues, that the rational and the ephod cannot be separated, when the ruler excels with such learning and such zeal for works that he leaves nothing imperfect of the things he has known are to be done, and does not by carelessness deprive what he has done of the virtue of uprightness. For the vestments of the high priest slip down and are moved from one another if a lesser watch of the heart soils the beauty of work, or the integrity of action does not follow the chastity of thought. But that they may not be loosed, the priest has on the rational two little chains of the purest gold, that is, the continuance of chaste and unfeigned love firmly fixed to the heart, which never allows hand and tongue to depart from the equity of pure sense. And well two, that in the things also which pertain to the relief of a brother's need he may walk adorned. And well is the work of charity signified by golden chains, because as a chain is woven of many small rods of gold, so charity is perfected by the manifold working of the virtues. Which small rods the Apostle sets out, saying: "Charity is patient, is kind. Charity envieth not" etc. The priest has golden rings, from which the chains hang, that is, the continual remembrance of the never-ending brightness in heaven, from which remembrance alone it comes that the bonds of charity remain continual for us. He has two hooks standing out in the corners of the ephod, into which the chains are put, that is, in the beginning of good work let him have a firm intention of pleasing God, which is fit in all things for receiving and holding in itself the love of God and neighbour, and, whether prosperity or adversity befall, never slackens the most wholesome reins of pious devotion. For this is for the priest to have on each shoulder hooks which receive the chains of the rational: in prosperity and adversity to bear a zeal fixed on pleasing God, and by its intention to be made firm in the love of God and neighbour. The golden chains, then, which are brought out from the tops of the rational, put themselves into the hooks of the ephod. For when the mind rationally tastes of the brightness of inner light, at once the eagerness of working well receives it with embrace, lest perhaps the most beautiful garment of the rational slip from the breast of the priest, if the hook of good action, hastening, does not hold it.
04_marg1637: That the ephod was fastened with the girdle, of which it is said in what follows: And over it he put the ephod, which, binding it with the girdle, he fitted to the rational, shows plainly that continence is the keeper of good works. Of which it is said: "Let your loins be girt, and lamps burning" etc. The loins girt, namely, by continence; the lamps burning, by the working of the virtues.
04_marg1638: WITH A VIOLET FILLET etc. BEDE. The violet fillets by which both garments of the priest are coupled are the bindings of heavenly desire, which, tied into golden rings, bind the ephod with the rational, when, having known the light of the everlasting fatherland, we sigh for that glory, and that we may deserve to enter it, strive to serve in the tabernacle of the present Church with concordant faith and life and work and profession.
04_marg1639: AND AARON SHALL BEAR etc. BEDE. Aaron bears the names of the children of Israel upon his breast for a memorial before the Lord for ever when the prelate never leaves off the care of those subject to him, but strengthens their life by consoling, rebuking, exhorting, and strives to commend it to the Lord's keeping by frequent prayers.
04_marg1640: The priest, when he enters the tabernacle, is commanded to bear on his breast twelve stones graven with the names of the children of Israel: this is our Redeemer, who, offering himself a sacrifice for us, when he had strong preachers in the beginning, bore twelve stones beneath the head in the first part of his body.
04_marg1641: The priest must bear the remembrance of the fathers on his breast, chiefly when he ministers at the altar, that where the ministry is more sacred he may adorn himself more skilfully with all zeal, with all industry of mind and of body, looking at the examples of the saints, that as their diligent imitator he may present himself fit for the divine sight.
04_interl4421: that the priest may study to seek out and teach doctrine and truth
04_interl4422: that he may examine the causes of his subjects with regard to God alone, mingling no grudge
04_marg1642: AND THOU SHALT PUT etc. BEDE. That namely the priest may remember that by the priesthood received he was consecrated to the pursuits of seeking out doctrine and truth, not to minding and chewing over worldly business; but that what shone forth outwardly in figure on the vesture might glitter truly expressed within in the heart. Again doctrine and truth were put in the rational, that it might be shown that that vesture not only clothed the high priest of the law but also foretold the high priest of the gospel, namely Christ himself, of whom it is said: The law was given by Moses, grace and truth were made known by Jesus Christ. Or the apostles and all the heralds of the new grace. And he bears the judgment of the children of Israel on his breast in the sight of the Lord when he examines the causes of his subjects with regard to the inner judge alone, that he mingle no grudge in what he dispenses in God's stead.
04_marg1643: And thou shalt put in the rational etc. In what thing or metal the manifestation and truth was put upon the rational (since he says that such things are made on the priest's vesture as are made bodily) it is hard to find. They tell, however, that there was a stone whose colour imitated adversity or prosperity when the priest went into the Holy place. And this is what he says: And Aaron shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his breast, showing namely in that manifestation and truth what the Lord had judged concerning them; although it can be understood that the manifestation and truth were letters set upon the logion.
04_interl4426: heavenly work to the end of life
04_interl4427: that the beginning of good work may be supported by the strong root of the fear of God, and fortified against the snares of the devil
04_interl4428: with the completion, namely, of works
04_marg1644: AND THOU SHALT MAKE THE TUNICK etc. BEDE. The priest is clothed with a tunic reaching to the ankles, all of violet, that he may be admonished that heavenly work is not only to be begun but to be carried through to the end by all who wish to be saved. For to be clothed with a violet tunic down to the feet is to persist in good works to the end of life, according to that: "Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee the crown of life." And because we shall come to the perfection of good work with unwearied purpose only if we begin it with the fixed intention of the reward above, rightly is it added: In the midst whereof above shall be a hole for the head etc. The violet tunic has a most firm opening for the head, and a border woven of itself, that it may not easily be broken, when the beginning of good work is proved to be supported by the strong root of the fear of the Lord and fortified against all the snares of the ancient enemy. Such a border clothes and adorns the priest's neck round about when it gives the ruler confidence in preaching heavenly things: this, that he has not only lived rightly in the course of his life but also took his beginning from uprightness, as Samuel, Jeremias, John, who, filled with spiritual grace from infancy itself, were also set apart in the order of doctors. For because the voice is in the neck, by the neck the practice of speaking rightly is expressed. As is wont to be made in the outmost parts of garments: as works by garments, so the completion of works is figured by the outmost parts of garments. Or the outmost parts of garments are our last cares, by which the faithful, when they are compelled to end their life, strive more earnestly to purge themselves of every stain of evil with fear and trembling, taking care lest, brought before the strict judge, they be cast out into the exterior darkness for the filthy habit of vices; but that they may appear clothed, as the elect of God, with the bowels of mercy, benignity, humility, modesty, patience and charity, "which is the bond of perfection". The violet tunic therefore has a woven border at the head-opening, as is wont to be made in the outmost parts of garments, when an excellent doctor begins the work of the virtues from so great a perfection as another by long labour scarcely ever reaches, and walks every hour with his God with as great fear of service as another, about to die and to enter the last judgment, would scarcely have enough of. But because the whole perfection of the priest consists in works and the doctrine of truth, according to that: "Jesus began to do and to teach", rightly is it added: "And beneath at the feet of the same tunick" etc.
04_marg1645: AND THOU SHALT MAKE THE TUNICK etc. He calls it the tunic of the ephod, part of which was covered by the ephod, to distinguish it from the tunic that was underneath, of linen, which he mentioned above, saying: "And these shall be the vestments that they shall make: a rational and an ephod, a tunick and a strait linen garment" etc. The inner one was of linen, fine linen, which is known to be the noblest kind of flax. But the outer tunic was all violet, admitting nothing of another colour; by whose uniform appearance it is taught what the life of the priest ought to be, namely intent on the desires above, having its conversation in heaven, and looking for the coming of the Saviour. Which, like the fine linen one, reached to the feet. Whence each was called in Greek poderis, that it might be shown that in the priestly life nothing low and base should remain, but that all he does should be most precious as with an ethereal colour, and all his members from head to feet ought to be covered with the grace of the virtues.
04_interl4429: that the priest may come to so great an excellence of conversation that nothing may appear in him but the brightness and grace and varied flower of good works, and that he may bring forth only their most sweet sound
04_interl4430: the manifold working of the virtues surrounded by the one defence of charity
04_interl4431: that every word of the priest may resound with the brightness of the light above
04_marg1646: AND BENEATH etc. GREGORY. When the ruler prepares himself to speak, he considers how cautiously he speaks, lest by speaking without order he cause the hearts of the hearers to err, and, desiring to seem wise, foolishly tear apart the framework of unity. Whence: Have salt in you, and have peace among you. For he who strives to speak wisely, let him fear lest by his eloquence unity be confounded. Whence: "Not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise" etc. Hence it is that pomegranates are joined to the bells. For by pomegranates the unity of faith is signified, because as in a pomegranate many seeds within are guarded by one rind, so the unity of faith covers the innumerable peoples of the Church, whom a diversity of merits holds within. Well therefore is it said: Have salt in you, and have peace among you etc.; as if it were said to the priests by the vesture: Join pomegranates to the bells, that through all that you say you may hold the unity of faith with careful observance.
04_marg1647: Beneath, at the feet of the tunic, are made as it were pomegranates and bells round about, when the priest has come to so great an excellence of devout conversation that nothing may be seen in him but brightness and grace and the varied flower of good works: that when he opens his mouth nothing else may be heard but the most sweet sound of these. For because in a pomegranate many seeds within are covered by one rind, rightly by pomegranates is signified the manifold working of the virtues covered on every side by the one defence of charity. And the likeness of the pomegranates is made of violet, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and fine twisted linen; by which four colours what variety of virtues is signified has been said above. And with these bells are mingled between, that neither the work of the priest may disagree with what he speaks, nor the sound of the tongue stray from the uprightness of work. Whence it is beautifully added: So that there shall be another golden bell and a pomegranate. For golden bells are inserted in the violet tunic and surround it on every side when all his speech resounds with the brightness of the light above, and the same sound, as if firmly fixed in the violet tunic, is commended to the minds of the hearers by the loftiness of his works also. And there are two pomegranates about each bell when all he speaks is confirmed by good acts and fixed more firmly in the heart of the hearers, and all he does is brought forth, how reasonable it is, by the discreet sound of speech.
04_marg1648: We can understand in the twelve gems of the rational that the sun of justice fills all our times and all the quarters of the world with his light, as the visible sun is wont to traverse the zodiac and go round the whole in twelve months. For this too, that the four rows in the rational have three stones each, agrees with the order of the turning year, which is divided into four seasons of three months each. And in the Scriptures the whole time of our salvation, in which we strive for an eternal reward, is wont to be called a year. For Christ, according to Isaias, was sent "to preach the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of reward". Of the same year David also says: "Thou shalt bless the crown of the year of thy goodness."
04_marg1649: Or, as was said above, he bore twelve gems, that is, three times four, that he might admonish all doctors to have the works of justice, which are contained in the four principal virtues, with the faith of the Trinity, and to commend them to their disciples. He bore also seventy-two golden bells with as many pomegranates, that he might show that the same faith and working of justice would lead the whole world from the darkness of errors and vices to the true light. For three days and nights have seventy-two hours, in which the sun, traversing above and below, goes round the world three times. Well therefore was this number of bells and pomegranates, with diversity of colour, set on the high priest's tunic, because Christ, "the sun of justice", was to enlighten the whole world, and to give the true faith, which is in the knowledge and confession of the Trinity, and good working, which is in the splendour of various virtues.
04_interl4434: For he will die if he does not preach so as to be heard by God and by men.
04_marg1650: THAT THE SOUND MAY BE HEARD etc. GREGORY. The priest going in or coming out dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes against himself the wrath of the hidden judge if he goes without the sound of preaching. And fittingly are the bells written to be set on his vestments. For the vestments of the priest are right works. Whence: "Let thy priests be clothed with justice." Bells therefore cling to his vestments, that the works of the priest themselves also may proclaim the way of life together with the sound of the tongue.
04_marg1651: That the sound may be heard etc. The priest going in and coming out dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes against himself the wrath of the hidden judge if he goes without the sound of preaching. But if we wish to attend to the words of Josephus, who says that there were seventy-two pomegranates and bells of the same number, it agrees with this mystery, that it has marked about the feet the number of the seventy-two disciples. For as the number twelve of the apostles began the degree of episcopal dignity, so the seventy-two disciples, who were themselves also sent to preach, signify the degree of the lesser priesthood, which is called the presbyterate. Whence the number of these is figured in the last part of the priestly habit, that in the first. And if anyone wishes to interpret mystically the numbers of both orders: Aaron bore twelve gems on his breast to signify that the time was at hand in which the faith of the Trinity would be preached in all parts of the four-cornered world.
04_interl4435: this the highest and excelling all the ornaments
04_interl4436: for the cleanness of heart and body in which we lay up and bear the mysteries of redemption
04_marg1652: THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO A PLATE OF etc. BEDE. The golden plate on the forehead of the high priest, on which was graven Holy to the Lord, or Holy of the Lord (as is said in what follows), is more sacred than the other vestments, because as the divine power is above all creatures, so his name must pass beyond the rest of the high priest's adornment, and, as sanctifying all things, hold the chief seat. And it signifies the confidence of our profession, which we bear on the forehead, the Apostle saying: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." And rightly this alone in the whole habit of the high priest is of gold only, that it might show the cleanness of heart or body in which we ought to lay up or bear the mysteries of our redemption. Or the priest bears Holy of the Lord inscribed in gold on his forehead, showing that we ought so to venerate and embrace the passion of the Lord by which we have been redeemed as to know that the brightness of the divine majesty in him, by which we were created, is likewise to be confessed: so confessing the death of the humanity assumed as to acknowledge that the same rose again.
04_marg1653: HOLY TO THE LORD etc. BEDE. That the holy and venerable name is commanded to be graven on the plate signifies that which among the Hebrews is written with four vowel letters, that is, ioth heth vav he, which is interpreted ineffable, not because it cannot be spoken, but because it cannot be defined by the sense and understanding of a creature, according to that: "The peace of God which surpasseth all understanding keep your hearts and minds" etc. And elsewhere: "Great is the Lord and exceedingly to be praised" etc. And well on the forehead of the high priest with four letters signifying as many parts of the Lord's cross, which we bear on the forehead.
04_marg1654: The ineffable name of the Lord, consisting of four letters: he, namely, which is interpreted this, ioth, which is beginning, heth, which is of passion, vav, that is, of life. Which as a whole sounds: this is the beginning of the passion of life; because Christ is the beginning of the life lost in Adam, which he restored by his passion.
04_marg1655: We bear the same Holy of the Lord graven in gold on our forehead when, purged from the filth of the vices which we had from our first parent, we receive back the image and likeness of the Creator to which we were created, and do not hide it, but publish it by deeds and words. According to that: As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of the heavenly. Whence also elsewhere: Stripping yourselves of the old man with his deeds, put on the new, who is renewed according to the image of him that created him. And John says: Having his name, and the name of his Father, written in their hearts. Since therefore all who follow the Lamb ought to have this name on the very forehead of their profession, how much more the priests who lead the Lord's flock, who ought to show to all an example of virtue?
04_marg1656: AND THOU SHALT TIE IT etc. The plate which contains Holy of the Lord is tied with a violet fillet to the high priest's mitre when we are strengthened in faith by the hope of heavenly rewards, which violet signifies, and keep more closely, unstained, the sacraments of our redemption, or the image and likeness of our Creator and Redeemer, than which we have known no other way of salvation to be. Of the mitre it will be said in its place.

04_marg1657: AND AARON SHALL BEAR etc. BEDE. The priest bears the iniquities in the gifts and offerings which the children of Israel have offered to the Lord and sanctified, when for the fruits of worthy penance, that is, alms and the other works of justice which penitents do, he absolves from the guilt of crimes. These things the divine institution figured in the habit of the high priest as so to be done, and taught plainly in words. But alas, some receive offerings, nay exact them, and neither carry away nor chastise the iniquities of the people, though they ought to take carnal things only for this, that they minister spiritual things. But because he can labour effectively for his subjects, preach and supplicate the Lord, whose mind is always endowed with the remembrance of the divine name, it is fittingly added: "And the plate shall be always on his forehead" etc.
04_interl4443: AUGUSTINE: This signifies the confidence of a good life, which he alone who is truly and perfectly a priest, not in signification but in truth, has, and he alone can take away sins.

04_marg1658: AND THE PLATE SHALL BE etc. BEDE. If the plate written with the name of God shall always be on the forehead of Aaron, the Lord will be pleased with the children of Israel; because when the doctor has faithfully subjected himself to the divine service with pure mind, his subjects, kindled by his examples and warnings, hasten to live rightly and to win the grace of the inner judge.
04_interl4447: This is the strait linen garment with which the priest is clothed, when he so keeps the purpose of continence that the flesh does not lust against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh.
04_marg1659: BEDE. Why the linen garment is called strait, or is commanded to be girt with fine linen, has been set out above. But now it must be added that soldiers are wont to have linen garments, which they call shirts, so fitted to the limbs and tight that they are unhindered in aiming the javelin, holding the shield, swinging the sword, and wherever need may draw them; such as Joab also is read to have had when he slew Amasa, tight, namely, to the measure of his body. So the priests also, ready for the ministry of God, use this tunic, that having the beauty of the clothed they may run about with the speed of the naked. This tunic, like the violet one, reaches down to the feet, and it too is called in Greek poderis, that is, reaching to the ankles. Its meaning is ready to hand: for since it is known that by flax or fine linen the continence and chastity of the body are signified, the priests have a strait linen garment, or a tunic of fine linen, when they keep the purpose of continence not feebly and with loose mind, but with such urgency that the flesh wages no war against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. They have a strait linen garment when their soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord, and their heart and flesh rejoice with companionable kinship in the living God. This linen garment is not only strait but also poderis, that is, coming down to the feet, when continence is not forcibly laid on some one member, but is delightfully completed in the whole body. For this linen garment ought to bind the hands and arms of the priest, lest he do anything useless; the breast, lest he think anything vain; the belly, lest he be gluttonous; the members below the belly, lest by wantonness they corrupt the whole beauty of the priestly habit; the knees, lest they grow sluggish from urgency in prayer; the legs and feet, lest they run to evil. Let the priest therefore first be clothed with the strait linen garment, that he may restrain the body from wicked works and the mind from depraved thoughts. Let him then take the violet tunic, that besides the outline of saving continence he may equally beautify body and soul with the habit of spiritual virtues. But because there are five senses of the body, four of which belong properly to the head, the fifth common to the whole body, this tunic, which we have said is both, properly designates the act of continence and justice. And next it is shown by the habit of the high priest how the innocence or sanctification of the other four senses also is to be cared for, when it is said: "And thou shalt make a fine linen mitre" etc.
04_interl4448: that all the senses of the head may be consecrated to God
04_marg1660: How this was made Josephus tells thus: Above he wears a cap in the manner of a small helmet or casque, which is stretched over the top of the head and a little passes the middle of the crown; and it is such that it seems made of a woven linen, having fillets which, rolled up, are tied many times over, that it may not easily slip off. He says also that over this cap another covering was added, which hid the whole surface of the head, fitted, surely, lest it fall while the priest laboured about the sacrifices; but of what colour it was he does not show. This of the lesser priests. But of the high priest's mitre he says thus: The high priest will have a cap made in like manner as the other priests, and another sewn over it of variegated violet. And a golden crown is put about it, made in three tiers, above which there rises in the middle of the forehead as it were a little golden stalk, like the herb which among us is called achanus, which the Greeks call vossamus. And a little after, having described its wonderful variety, he added: And it has a flower like the plantain, and round about the whole crown is chased with these flowers, from the back of the head to each temple. On the forehead it does not have this, but there is a golden plate which has the name of God inscribed in sacred letters. Of the second covering and the golden crowns of the high priests Scripture seems to be silent. But it mentions the crowns briefly in what follows thus: "They made also tunicks of woven work for Aaron and his sons, and mitres with their little crowns of fine linen", but of what material they were it did not say. For when it says: "And mitres with their little crowns of fine linen", it could be understood that both were made of fine linen, did not Josephus say that the crowns were of gold, who, while the temple and the observance of the law still stood, since he was of priestly stock, could know every manner of the priestly vestment, not by reading only, but by seeing; but whether the little crowns were of fine linen or of gold, it is plain that they were made with the mitres. Now let us speak briefly of the figure. The priests have mitres of fine linen with little crowns who so keep sight, hearing, taste and smell in chastity that they hope to receive from it the crown of life. For he who so studies continence or good works that he neglects the rewards of retribution has a fine linen mitre without a crown, because he shows to men the appearance of virtue as a crown, but has no reward from the Lord. If then the little crowns were of gold, they signify the brightness of perpetual light; or if of fine linen, the everlasting immortality of the body. And rightly the priest with stoles of fine linen bore crowns added above, that in continence he may meditate on eternal rewards, and in preaching continence or good working may promise the joys of beatitude above; lest, laying the weight of labour without hope of reward, he make the sweet yoke and light burden of Christ harsh and hard to his hearers.
04_marg1661: AND A FINE LINEN MITRE etc. BEDE. The mitre, which is called tiara and cidaris, covered and adorned the head of the high priest, that he might be admonished to have all the senses of the head consecrated to God: lest either the eyes should see vanity, or the ears receive the reproach of a neighbour, or the mouth abound with malice, the tongue frame deceit; lest surfeiting and drunkenness weigh down the heart, or the smell embrace the harlot's bed sprinkled with myrrh and aloes and cinnamon; but that the eyes might see equity, the ears be inclined to the words of prudence, the words of the Lord be sweet to his palate, and, while breath remained, he might not speak iniquity, might not touch the polluted, but, cleansed from all defilement of flesh and spirit, might perfect sanctification in the fear of God.

04_interl4450: of whose making it is said more fully in what follows: "And they made the girdle of fine twisted linen" etc.
04_marg1662: AND A GIRDLE. BEDE. Of the making of the girdle it is written: They made the girdle of fine twisted linen, violet, purple and scarlet twice dyed, of embroidered work. This girdle, as Jerome writes from Josephus, was woven round, in the likeness of a serpent's skin which is cast off in old age, so that you would think it a long purse. And it was woven with a woof of scarlet, purple, violet, and a warp of fine linen, for beauty and comeliness, and so distinguished with variegated art that you would judge the various flowers and gems not woven by the craftsman's hand but added. And it had a breadth of four fingers; which girdle the high priest properly used, and with it the violet tunic and likewise the ephod were bound. For in what follows it is said plainly of the joining of the ephod and the rational: These answered so to one another before and behind, that the ephod and the rational were bound together, fastened to the girdle and coupled more firmly with rings, which a violet fillet joined, lest they should hang loose and be moved from one another. And no one doubts that the girdle and band to which the ephod was bound girt the violet tunic, which is also called the tunic of the ephod. For all that has been said thus far pertains to the habit of the high priest. Then follow the girdles and other vestments of his sons, when it is said: "Moreover for the sons of Aaron thou shalt prepare linen tunicks" etc. And it must be said of the girdle of the high priest, which was made of those four noblest colours worthy of God, that the high priest would well have such a one, who must always be girt with a singular beauty of virtues. Well did he walk girt with the varied flower of shining colours, because as it is necessary that another be girt with the industry of continence, lest the flesh, fighting against the spirit, disturb the inner quiet of the mind, so the high priest, every lust of body and soul being now tamed, ought to be surrounded with the very glory of the virtues, that after the example of that flower which came forth from the root of Jesse, that is, Christ, justice may be the girdle of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins.
04_marg1663: THOU SHALT PREPARE TUNICKS etc. The priests have linen tunics when they dedicate the whole body to the whiteness of chastity. They gird the tunics with girdles when they look round upon that same chastity with watchful guard of mind, lest by the consciousness of it they become more slothful toward good works, lest by boasting of chastity they lessen even its merit. For he who is clothed with a tunic reaching to the ankles, if he walks without a girdle, the tunic slips down and, leaving the body, gives entrance to winds and cold, and, the steps being hindered, slows the use of walking, or makes those who tread on it fall: so also the chastity of the flesh often takes away the chastity of the heart, while they persist more sluggishly in good works, when they look ahead less, because chastity avails apart from other goods, but with these joined to it acquires glory and beauty. Chastity of the flesh did not profit the foolish virgins, who lacked the light of inner purity. Let them be girt therefore with linen tunics, that they may have chastity. Let them be girt with girdles, lest chastity be slack, lest it open entrance to the wind of pride, lest it make charity grow cold, lest the boasting of presumption hinder good works, lest, the course of the virtues being hindered, it grow vile, polluted with the filth of concupiscence, and at length drive to ruin by pride. And, being girt, let them take mitres on their heads, that besides the watchful guard of bodily chastity, sight, hearing, taste and smell may be kept worthily for God.
04_marg1664: AND WITH ALL THESE THINGS THOU SHALT VEST etc. BEDE. With all these things Aaron and his sons were to be clothed, but distinctly, so that he himself should use all these, but the sons the last three which are properly assigned to them, when it is said: "Moreover for the sons of Aaron thou shalt prepare linen tunicks" etc.
