04_marg1665: THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO LINEN BREECHES etc. BEDE. The breeches which are made to cover the nakedness of the body or flesh properly designate that portion of chastity which holds back from the conjugal union, without which no one can either receive the priesthood or be consecrated to the ministry of the altar: that is, if he has not either remained a virgin or dissolved the bonds of marriage; which is commanded to no one of necessity, but is to be offered to God voluntarily. Whence: "All men take not this word." And: "He that can take, let him take it." And a little after he promises to those who have left wife or other kin and the hindrances of the world for his sake a hundredfold in this world, and in the world to come life everlasting. Whence Moses is not commanded to clothe Aaron and his sons with this vestment, as is said of the former ones: Thou shalt vest Aaron thy brother with all these etc. But: Thou shalt make linen breeches, to cover the flesh of their nakedness etc. Thou shalt make breeches for the high priest and his sons; thou shalt teach the rule of chastity; thou shalt make known that those who are to enjoy the priesthood must abstain from the embrace of a wife. Yet thou shalt lay the yoke of this continence forcibly on no one; but whoever wish to become priests and serve the altar, let them of their own will cease to be servants of wives. And when they have done this, so that, having once taken up the purpose of continence, they have consented to be ministers of the sanctuary and the altar, the divine law will be at hand, which, as it were laying on the rest of the habit befitting priests, will instruct abundantly how they ought to live or teach, and, rejoicing at their spontaneous devotion, will add above the beauty worthy of the priesthood: of wisdom, patience, meekness, mercy, spiritual zeal, humility, the fear of the Lord, and the rest of such adornment. Otherwise "being guilty of iniquity they die", if namely, living wantonly, they usurp the priestly degree. Which sense is confirmed by the following words, when it is said: And when thou hast washed the father with his sons with water etc., as far as: and they shall be priests to me by a perpetual ordinance. For neither here is anything commanded about the breeches to be received from Moses; whence it is plain that Aaron himself and his sons had first put on this kind of vestment, and so came in to be washed, vested, anointed and consecrated by the hand of Moses. Where it is to be noted that Moses, about to consecrate them, first washed them with water, and so put on them the habit of the priest, because it is necessary that he who is to be promoted to the office of the altar should wash himself with streams of tears or compunction greater than usual, that the cleaner he has come to receive the degree, the more perfectly he may fulfil it when received.

04_marg1672: THOU SHALT CLOTHE AARON etc. BEDE. It is to be noted that whereas in Exodus Aaron is declared to be clothed with eight vestments, in Leviticus a ninth seems to be added: namely the girdle with which the linen tunic was girt before the violet one was put on. For so it is written: And when he had washed them, he vested the high priest with the strait linen garment, girding him with the girdle, and putting on him the violet tunick; and over it he put the ephod, which, binding with the girdle, he fitted to the rational.
04_marg1673: It is to be noted that the four excellent colours of which the habit of the priest was made are fitted by a fitting comparison to as many elements of the world. Fine linen or flax to the earth, because it springs from it; purple to the waters, because it is dyed from sea shellfish. Violet and scarlet to the air and fire, because of the likeness of colour. The scarlet twice dyed, because fire is of twofold power: for it shines and burns. The Hebrews say that the high priest bore in his habit the figure of all the elements, because, sacrificing, he ought to pray for the whole world; to which we perhaps can add that in every man the figure of all the elements is contained: of fire in warmth, of air in breath, of waters in moisture, of earth in the solidity of the members. Whence man is called in Greek microcosmos, that is, 'lesser world'. And gold in the same habit signifies the rational power of the inner man. Whence on it properly was written Holy of the Lord, because by this alone does he rise to the knowledge of the Creator. Whence: In the inner man, that Christ may dwell by faith in our hearts. And therefore Scripture shows us the high priest of the Old Testament so vested, that the high priest of our time may know that he ought to intercede for the whole human race, but chiefly for those who have known the truth and bear the sign of faith on their foreheads: I desire therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men: for kings, and for all that are in high station. But if in the high priest whom Moses consecrates we understand Christ, rightly does he have in his habit the figure of the whole world and of man together: for he upholds all things by the word of his power. And he is "the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sins of the world", and a priest for ever, illustrious with every adornment of holiness, not which, born in the flesh, he received by the exercise of labour, but which, incarnate in the womb of the Virgin, he had at once, the grace of the Holy Ghost going before. Of whose priesthood the Apostle says: "But this, for that he continueth for ever, hath an everlasting priesthood" etc. Commending also the vestments and adornments of the virtues, he says: For it was fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, undefiled etc. And he had on his head a plate of gold, and on it Holy of the Lord engraved, because he came in the name of the Father, saying: "I am in the Father, and the Father in me"; and: "He that seeth me seeth the Father also."

04_marg1677: AUGUSTINE. How does he say that it is proper to this one alone to enter the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy places, since those things too which are outside the veil by which the holy of holies is veiled are called holy, and that too is called the tabernacle of the testimony where the holy things are, that is, the table and the candlestick, where the following priests also minister at the table and the candlestick and the altar itself? How does he speak of one successor of Aaron who enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy places? For if he had said 'to minister in the holy of holies', there would be no question. For into that, where the ark of the testimony is, the high priest alone entered; unless perhaps by the very fact that he says that one enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy places, he does not wish it to be understood of the holy of holies, because those too are called holy. For not all things that are holy can also be called holy of holies, but the things that are holy of holies are certainly holy. And this one, who once a year went into the holy of holies, signifies Christ. And that which was prefigured in the holy of holies, that over the ark which held the Law there was the propitiatory, where the mercy of God is understood to be signified, by which he becomes propitious to the sins of those who do not fulfil the Law: this seems to be signified also in the very vesture of the priest, which itself also signifies the sacraments of the Church, who on the logion, that is, the rational, placed on the breast of the priest, set judgments; and on the plate, the sanctification and abolishing of sins; as if the rational on the breast were like the ark in which the Law was, and the plate on the forehead like the propitiatory which was over the ark, and that in both that might be kept which is written: "Mercy exalteth itself above judgment."

04_marg1678: THOU SHALT MAKE ALSO AN ALTAR etc. BEDE. The commands for the consecration of Aaron and his sons being fulfilled, Scripture returns to give commands also about the making of the altar of incense, on which Aaron was to burn the daily incense. If in the altar of holocaust, of which it was spoken above, the life of the just is generally signified, who daily crucify their flesh with its vices and concupiscences and offer it as a living victim, what does this altar, made for burning incense, designate but the special life of the just? For not in vain were the flesh of animals burnt on that, incense burnt on this; but on that were figured those who do not walk according to the desires of the flesh, but, as it were sacrificing these to the Lord, dedicate all the senses of the body to his will through the fire of the Spirit. But on this are figured those who, with greater perfection of mind, all the allurements of the flesh being quenched, offer to the Lord the solid vows of prayers: having nothing of the flesh to resist, nothing of the consciousness of sin to trouble their minds, longing, amid the outpouring of sweet tears, to come and appear before the face of the Lord. Whence this altar was set within, near the veil and the ark, that one outside before the tabernacle, because the former shine forth before all in the sight of the Church as an example of virtues; the latter, by the ardour of a loftier desire, draw near even in the body to the contemplation of the beatitude to come.
04_marg1679: BEDE. Fittingly also the altar of incense, the more it excelled in the brightness of its metal, the less it was in size: for the holier, the fewer.
04_interl4532: the hearts of the elect, fortified by the firmness of true faith
04_marg1680: BEDE. Fittingly is each altar commanded to be made of setim wood, like the white thorn and incorruptible, because there is one firmness of true faith, by which the hearts of all the elect must be fortified and prepared to receive the fire of love and to offer to God the libations of the virtues. For the Apostle says to all in general: "Let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God"; as if to say: let us take away from ourselves the thickets of vices and the stings of tickling prickings, which the earth of our body has made to spring up for us from the sin of the first transgression, and, cutting them as with the axe of chastisement, let us cultivate our inner and outer man, that we may be worthy, having received the fire of the Holy Ghost, to offer the victim of the virtues in the sight of God. Fittingly one fire, not different, burned the victims on that and the frankincense on this, because there is one spirit, who quickens the minds of all the faithful with the varied grace of his gifts.
04_interl4533: the long-suffering of patience, as was said in the exposition of the altar of holocaust
04_interl4534: the perseverance of the saints in good work
04_marg1681: HAVING A CUBIT etc. BEDE. The length and breadth of the altar is of one cubit, because the perfect bear temporal evils with the sole regard of perpetual refreshment, and bestow through charity on their neighbours what good things they can. Again, because charity is patient and kind: patient, to bear injury done by a neighbour; kind, to bestow the office of piety even on the one who does injury.
04_interl4536: that it may be stable and firm on every side
04_interl4537: with the hope of heavenly rewards, namely of soul and of body
04_interl4538: because meanwhile there is the rest of souls, and in the resurrection also the beatitude of bodies
04_marg1682: BEDE. Rightly is the altar of incense made foursquare in length and breadth, because the soul of the perfect, the virtues being leagued with one another, is as able to bear a brother as to love him, and as able to love as to bear. And it has two cubits in height, because the elect hope to receive a double reward in the future, one of souls, the other of bodies. Whence: In their land they shall receive double, everlasting joy shall be unto them.
04_interl4539: They signify the eminence of the virtues and of faith, by which we overcome the assaults of the devil, saying: "Through thee we will push down our enemies with our horn."
04_marg1683: HORNS SHALL GO OUT OF IT etc. BEDE. The horns signify the eminence of faith and virtue, by which the Church overcomes the wars of vices. Whence: "And I will break all the horns of sinners: but the horns of the just shall be exalted." Whence in the law only horned animals are decreed to be clean and fit to eat. For those which chew the cud and divide the hoof are known to be horned, because they only can be incorporated into the Church of God by spiritual union who are proved unconquered against the wars of vices by the strength of faith and virtue. And the horns go out of the altar of incense itself when the elect do not show the works of the virtues to the face of men in appearance only, but exercise them from the inner root of the mind with fixed and unmoved affection. But on the other hand the hypocrites, with horns borrowed from elsewhere, having an appearance of godliness, deny the power thereof.
04_interl4540: because the perfect shine with the light of inner wisdom, and show in all they do that the splendour of charity is in them, and that they think on and seek before all things the kingdom of God and his justice
04_marg1684: BEDE. Fittingly is that one commanded to be clothed with brass, this with gold. For brass is more sounding and lasting than other metals; but gold, as much as it is surpassed in sound, so much does it surpass the other metals in brightness. Whence rightly the brazen altar, on which flesh was burnt and the blood of victims poured out, signifies those who, the pleasures of the flesh being tamed and as it were sacrificed to God, carry through perseveringly the way they have begun, and sound it forth to their neighbours to be kindled by frequent words of preaching. But gold signifies those who are enlightened by a fuller grace of the brightness above, but open less to others what they taste in secret of the inner sincerity: they are less able to utter with how great sweetness of God they are refreshed in the hidden place of his face.
04_interl4541: the confidence of the strength of the just
04_marg1685: AS WELL THE GRATE etc. BEDE. Well are the grate of the altar, the walls and the horns clothed with gold. For the grate was within, in the middle of the altar, prepared to receive the incense. But the walls appeared outside; the horns too, appearing outside, stood out higher with a special peak. The grate is gilded when the grace of Christ shines in the inner man through faith. The walls are gilded when the same grace of the Lord's love is spread abroad outwardly through good works. The horns are gilded when the confidence of the strength of the just, by which they have learned either to bear the adversaries of truth strongly through patience, or to repel or correct them wisely through prudence, glitters in all things with the brightness of inner light. And because such can say: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" etc., rightly is it added: "And thou shalt make a crown of gold" etc.
04_interl4542: that the saints may await eternal rewards for the good things they remember they have done
04_interl4543: that all things may be shown worthy of heavenly reward, and nothing remain to be corrected by purgatorial fire after release from the flesh
04_marg1686: AND THOU SHALT MAKE A CROWN etc. BEDE. The altar of incense has a crown round about in those who are less in merits and do not dare to declare openly that the reward of the good fight and service and faith is laid up for them: yet they do all things with the intention of well pleasing God, but in the hope of receiving reward.
04_interl4544: the love of God and neighbour, which never falleth away
04_interl4545: the sayings of the fathers who went before, by which, lifted up from the earth, they are advanced to heavenly things
04_interl4546: because the intention of the just directs them to the entrance of heaven
04_marg1687: AND TWO RINGS etc. BEDE. In these rings the four books of the Gospel can be taken, by whose faith and doctrine the saints are carried, and, lifted up from earthly thoughts, are borne through the wilderness of this life with the daily fruits of works to the heavenly fatherland, as has been set out of the altar of holocaust, the ark and the table. But there were four rings there; here two are said to be made on each side. There therefore the number of the evangelists more plainly; here another mystery, which looks to the love of God and neighbour. For the altar is surrounded with golden rings on each side because the heart of the elect is made firm on this side and that by the love of God and neighbour. Which is compared to rings, because when prophecy and knowledge and tongues shall cease, charity will never cease. There are two rings on each side because each commandment of charity is distinguished by a twofold virtue. For love of God is perfected by sincerity of faith and cleanness of life. "For without faith it is impossible to please God", and "faith without works is dead". Whence: But my just man liveth by faith, that is, he who has the works of justice with the faith of truth comes to life. Brotherly love too consists in patience and kindness. Whence: "Charity is patient, is kind" etc. And elsewhere: Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you. Into these rings gilded bars are put, that the altar may be carried, when such receive with the ready bosom of the mind the bright examples and sayings of the fathers, by which, raised from earthly things, they are caught up to the love of eternal things. And that in merit and mind they draw near to heavenly things, what follows shows: "And thou shalt set the altar" etc.
04_interl4547: heaven, which the Lord entered when death was overcome
04_interl4549: The altar stands before the propitiatory by which the testimony is covered when the saints draw near to the vision of God by purity of mind, who, though in a mortal body, have their conversation in heaven.
04_interl4550: because the saints daily contemplate Christ
04_interl4552: prayer; whence: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight."
04_interl4553: Christ, or the priests of our order
04_interl4555: because to the compunct it is sweet to weep and pray
04_interl4556: by calling on the help of God at the beginning of good work
04_marg1688: AND SHALL BURN INCENSE etc. BEDE. Incense or thymiama signifies prayer, according to that: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight." And elsewhere: "Golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints." And because Aaron, as was said above, signifies the high priest, that is, Christ, and the priests of our order, Aaron will burn sweet smelling incense on the altar in the morning, when Christ will stir up the hearts of the faithful, enlightened with the splendour of new grace, to the sweetness of prayer; or the sharers of his priesthood, by earnest exhortation, stir up the faithful to entreat the face of their Creator. The priest burns the incense not only in the morning but also in the evening. For in the morning incense is burnt, that at the beginning of every good which by God's inspiration we purpose to do, we may call on his help, by which we may complete it. In the evening, that when we complete what was well begun, we may give thanks to him from whom we began.
04_marg1689: AND SHALL BURN INCENSE etc. In the morning, the sun being risen, we see all things clearly round about; in the evening we are in darkness, and therefore we need the light of a lamp. By the morning therefore those sacraments or sayings of the Redeemer which we are able to discern clearly according to the order of human reason, after our small measure, and behold as it were in the day. But in those where human reason fails, and the authority of Scripture alone is to be sought, there the eye of the understanding is darkened as in the night. But the lamp of the word of God helps our feet, lest perhaps they stumble and stray from the way of truth. Whence Peter: "We have the more firm prophetical word, whereunto you do well to attend, as to a light that shineth in a dark place."
04_marg1690: IN THE MORNING WHEN HE SHALL DRESS etc. BEDE. In the morning Aaron burns incense on the altar when Christ inflames the hearts of the faithful with the grace of compunction in those sacraments which they can understand. He burns it also in the evening, when he places the lamps, when even from those things which they cannot yet grasp, since it is not doubted that they are holy and divine, he forms them to the love of heavenly things, where all things are laid open. The incense smells sweet when, touched from on high by sudden compunction, they delight to give themselves only to tears and prayers.
04_interl4560: because it is necessary that the mind after prayer and weeping beware of idle words or deeds, and keep itself in the same freshness of devotion even when prayer is ended; as it is said of Anna, namely: Her countenance was no more changed.
04_interl4561: nothing is to be asked in prayer but what God has commanded and has promised to give
04_marg1691: YOU SHALL NOT OFFER etc. BEDE. In what follows it is marked out by name of what spices this incense is to be compounded: namely stacte and onycha, galbanum of sweet savour, and the clearest frankincense; all of which are known to pertain to the signifying of the eternal goods to be sought chiefly from the Lord. Incense therefore of another composition than the Lord appointed is not to be offered on the golden altar, because in praying we ought to seek from the Lord nothing but what he himself commanded, who promised to give it, nor to believe anything else of him than he himself taught.
04_interl4562: which pertain to beginners, in whom carnal things are still to be sacrificed
04_interl4563: of wine, which signify the cup of doctrine, or the chalice of the passion, or the fervour of love
04_marg1692: No victim is to be offered upon it, nor libations poured. For all these pertain to the outer altar, which designates the life of beginners and of those who are advancing. For the life of the perfect is of such loftiness that nothing carnal is found in it to be sacrificed to the Lord. And the libations of wine designate the virtue of spiritual grace, namely either the cup of doctrine, or the chalice of the passion, or chiefly the fervour of love, or the receiving of the Holy Ghost himself, or something of this kind. But whenever the wine of libations is offered with the flesh of victims, it designates the holiness of those who still have something of carnal concupiscences which is opposed to purity of spirit and is kindled by spiritual fire on the altar of the heart. But the perfect, who can say: "For thee my flesh and my heart hath fainted away: thou art the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever", the libations of victims ceasing, which pertains to the brazen altar set outside, offer within on the golden altar only the spices of heavenly desire, because, secure of the remission of sins, they mourn only for the delay of the everlasting kingdom, and every night water their couch with the sweet streams of tears.
04_marg1693: We can interpret these altars so as to take the brazen one, on which flesh is burnt and the blood of victims poured out, as the whole Church of this time, in which no one is without sin, not even an infant of one day; there is no one who, born of the sin of transgression, has not need to be reborn in Christ and to be cleansed by the fire of his spirit. But the golden altar signifies Christ, who ineffably so took true flesh from Adam as to be free from the sin of Adam's flesh; whence both altars were made of the same kind of wood, but not both covered with gold. On this altar too nothing carnal was offered, but only spices, because Christ poured out prayers and tears not for his own errors but for our salvation. For as the ark placed within the veil signifies the man God sitting at the right hand of the majesty, so the altar placed outside the veil, but near its entrance, can express the same mediator of God and man, dwelling among men in his humanity, but by the power of his divinity entering the inner parts of heaven. The altar of incense stood in the sanctuary where the candlestick and the table were, because "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us". The ark stood within the veil, because Christ after his passion and resurrection was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God. Upon the horns of whose altar Aaron prays in the blood which was offered for sin, and makes atonement upon it, when the priests, praying for the people or for their own ignorance, trust that they are to be helped through the Son of God and saved through the sacrament of his passion. Whence: By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise always to God, that is to say, the fruit of lips confessing to his name; which can be taken of all the elect, the members, namely, of the high priest, who pray to the Father in spirit and in truth.
04_interl4567: the priest went daily into the Holy place to burn incense; but once a year with blood, with which he sprinkled the horns of the altar.
04_marg1694: AND SHALL PRAY etc. BEDE. Because Christ our priest offered his blood once in the year for the sins of all, when namely he preached the acceptable year of the Lord, that is, the whole time in which he deigns to join the Church to himself. Once also he gave to each believer the laver of baptism, in the mystery of his blood, for loosing the bonds of sins. And beautifully is he commanded to pray once a year with the blood of the oblation upon the horns of the altar, but to burn incense on it daily, because Christ, who daily renews the faithful, kindling them with the grace of inner compunction, once redeemed them by the victim of his blood when death was overcome. The faithful themselves too, who wash away daily sins with daily prayers and tears, rejoice that they have been once absolved from all sins in the sacrament of his passion. Aaron will pray upon the horns of the altar, because Christ not only prayed for men while dwelling among men, but also now, sitting at the right hand of the Father, intercedes for us. Dwelling also by faith in the hearts of the elect, while he stirs them up to pray, he is rightly said to pray. Aaron prays upon the horns of the altar when he commends the elect to the Father through the remembrance of the virtues they have practised. Lastly, as if touching the horns of the golden altar, he speaks of the devotion of the disciples: "Thine they were, whom thou gavest me out of the world, and to me thou gavest them; and they have kept thy word" etc. And he added: "I pray for them: I pray not for the world." And because for the merits and intercessions of lofty men the Lord has mercy on our weakness, rightly is it added: "And shall make atonement upon it in your generations."
04_interl4572: through the justice of the saints
04_interl4573: of Christ to be born it is said to the virgin mother: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" etc.
04_marg1695: AND SHALL MAKE ATONEMENT etc. BEDE. Aaron makes atonement upon the altar of incense when God is made propitious for the sake of the justice of the saints, which we seek as intercessor and patron for ourselves. Whence it is said to Ezechias: I will save this city, and will protect it for my own sake, and for David my servant's sake. As Moses, interceding for the people, made remembrance of the fathers, and, as if praying upon the horns of the altar, took care to appease the Lord, saying: Be appeased upon the wickedness of thy people, and remember Abraham, Isaac and Israel etc.
04_marg1696: AND THE LORD SPOKE etc. The altar of incense being described, there remains the description of the brazen laver in which the priests about to enter the tabernacle should wash their hands and feet; but one command is put first.
04_interl4574: that is: when thou hast numbered them, going on an expedition
04_interl4575: AUGUSTINE: this was punished in David, because God had not commanded it
04_interl4576: of all the elect, whose names are written in the book of life
04_interl4578: because they are perpetually damned who obtain the number of the faithful in name only
04_marg1697: BEDE. David forgot this precept when he numbered the people, and therefore by numbering brought a scourge upon the people itself. But mystically, the sum of the children of Israel signifies the sum of all the elect, whose names are written in heaven; and each gives a price to the Lord for their souls when they diligently serve him in good works; otherwise, being numbered, they will incur the scourge, because perpetual vengeance awaits those who, joined to the number of the faithful in name only, do not offer the Lord the perfect works of faith. Of such it is said: He shall not give to God his ransom, nor the price of the redemption of his soul. For the ransom of a man's soul are his riches.
04_interl4580: that is: to the family: for those who passed were named
04_interl4581: that is, ten obols, namely the observance of the Decalogue and the faith of Jesus Christ
04_interl4582: according to the will of the offerer
04_marg1698: BEDE. That is, ten obols, namely the observance of the decalogue and the faith of Jesus Christ. For he who rightly understands this knows that in it is all the multitude both of faith and of work and the promise of reward to come. Lastly, in the first three the love of God, in the seven following the love of neighbour is contained; and, the Apostle witnessing: Love is the fulfilling of the law. The name of Jesus also among the Hebrews and Greeks begins with ioth and iota, each of which is the mark of the number ten. And they offer ten obols as the price of the soul who, believing in Jesus Christ, bear on their forehead and in their profession the sign of his name, which begins from the number ten. Perhaps therefore it was said that one iota cannot pass from the law, because the virtue of the decalogue which is contained there, and the faith of the name which is signified there, can be corrupted by no disturbance of unbelievers.
04_interl4586: understanding the Law spiritually, and fulfilling it helped by the grace of the Gospel
04_marg1699: HE THAT IS COUNTED IN THE NUMBER etc. Twenty signifies the joining of both Testaments, namely of the law, which is written in five books, and of the Gospel, which is written in four: for four times five make twenty. From twenty years therefore each is counted in the number of the people of God, because he alone is worthy of the fellowship of the elect who, helped by the grace of the Gospel, fulfils according to his measure and capacity the decrees of the law spiritually understood, and awaits the eternal rewards promised in heaven.
04_interl4589: the Decalogue is laid on all equally
04_marg1700: THE RICH MAN SHALL NOT ADD etc. BEDE. Because whether one be great in merits and perfect, or little and set in the course of advancing in virtues, the law of the Decalogue, by which they are to love God and neighbour, is laid on all equally.
04_interl4594: in the remembrance of God, that he may deign to become propitious
04_marg1701: AND THE MONEY RECEIVED etc. BEDE. This is done when whatever good we do is kept in the eternal remembrance of our Creator and Judge, that from the fruits of the good things we have offered him he may become propitious to us. The same money is kept for the use of the tabernacle when by the works of the just both the manners and the acts of the faithful who follow are confirmed, and the lesser strive to become such as they know those to have been whom they hear to be reigning with the Lord. It is indeed to be noted that the money was to be given not according to the estimation of the crowd, but according to the standard of the temple. The standard of the temple is the ordering of the divine law, which the Lord commanded to be kept in his Church, and promises eternal rewards to those who keep it. If anyone strives to serve God according to the pleasure of human will, because he has not offered the money of devotion according to the standard of the temple, his oblation being rejected, he will be struck with the scourge of strict vengeance.
04_interl4595: Moses set this laver, because the law of God preached to all the faithful the grace of compunction
04_interl4596: "Every night I will wash my bed: I will water my couch with my tears."
04_interl4597: the unfailing washing of compunction and tears, with which priests and all the saints ought often to be washed
04_interl4598: the desire of the heavenly life
04_interl4599: "Every night I will wash my bed, with my tears" etc.
04_interl4600: because no one becomes highest of a sudden
04_interl4601: because there are two kinds of tearful compunction: namely for sins, and from desire of the heavenly fatherland
04_marg1702: AND THE LORD SPOKE etc. BEDE. In this laver (labium or labrum, for both are said) the water of baptism can be understood, by whose washing those who enter the doors of the Church must be cleansed. But because it was set between the tabernacle of the testimony and the altar of holocaust, and because the same priests were commanded to wash in it twice daily, that is, morning and evening, when they went in to the altar to offer incense to the Lord, whereas one is washed with the water of baptism once only, we more fittingly take this laver as the washing of compunction and tears, which we always need, chiefly when we come to minister the heavenly mysteries. For the altar of holocaust, on which the flesh of the victims was burnt to the Lord, signifies the quenching of carnal concupiscences by the fire of the Holy Ghost; but the altar of incense, the purity of those who, the allurements of the flesh being wholly put to sleep, shed tears of love only in the expectation and desire of entering heaven. Rightly is the laver set near the altar of holocaust, in which the priests, being washed, enter that tabernacle and burn incense to the Lord. For the state of tears and compunctions is distinguished in two ways: because first each one converted asks pardon weeping for his sins; and when he has long fulfilled this with worthy fruits of penance, secure of pardon, he longs with gaping desires for the time to be at hand when he may go in to see the face of the Creator, and does not bear without tears the length of this life or the delay of that, saying: "Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged" etc. And elsewhere: "My soul hath thirsted after the strong living God" etc. And a little after: "My tears have been my bread day and night" etc. The altar of holocaust therefore signifies the tears of penitents; the altar of incense, those of men rejoicing in the good things they have done with God's help, and desiring the rewards which they trust they will receive. Which weeping excels the former as much as gold excels brass, as much as the holy of holies, where the ark of the Lord was, excels the former tabernacle, in which were the candlestick and the table of the Lord. The laver was set near the altar of holocaust, in which those who went in to the altar of incense were washed, because no one becomes highest of a sudden, but, as merits advance, each must first overcome the wars of vices, and so obtain from God the compunction of tears, that he who shed bitter tears for fear of punishments may shed sweet tears for entrance into the kingdom.
04_marg1703: The laver was a vessel in which those washed who were about to enter the temple of God and to sacrifice, and to receive the holy vestments and put off their own, and likewise those about to go out; made of the mirrors of the women who watched at the entrance of the tabernacle.
04_marg1704: BEDE. The foot on which the laver was set signifies the desire of the heavenly life, the cause of which is so great that perfect men wash themselves with daily tears, and taste by sighing the joy of inner rest which they cannot by seeing. And that by this laver (which was set between the tabernacle and the altar) the tears of the perfect are figured these words testify: And water being put into it, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands in it etc. No one of the people is commanded to be washed there, but the high priest and his sons, that is, the priests of the lesser degree, because of great men, as the life is more perfect, so the compunction is loftier. But this compunction befits not the ministers of the altar alone. For Peter says to all the faithful: Be you also as living stones built up, a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices. And John: Blessed is he that hath part in the first resurrection. In these the second death hath no power. And what victims they ought to offer Paul shows, saying: I beseech you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice etc.
04_marg1705: SHALL WASH IN IT etc. Christ too was washed with the water of this laver before he went in to offer at the altar and burned the incense of his sacred body for our salvation on the altar of the cross: for he shed tears for love of us, as at the raising of Lazarus.
04_interl4610: The laver and the priesthood of Aaron have been destroyed, but what they signified remains for ever: in the life of the faithful the altar and the incense remain, as many other things which the law commanded to be celebrated perpetually.
04_interl4611: that is: to all the saints, because Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfil
04_interl4612: that is: to those who believe in him in whom Aaron believed. For this is the seed which the Lord hath blessed.
04_marg1706: LEST PERHAPS THEY DIE etc. BEDE. For eternal death is to be feared if anyone chosen for the ministry of the altar does not render the incense of prayers, but presumes to enter the most holy mysteries without the washing of compunction, and to handle the holy table of the Lord with common hands. Let them wash their hands and feet therefore in the water of the brazen laver, and so go to the altar; let them wash their acts and goings with tears, then put forth their hands to touch the mysteries of God, and set the going of their feet in the court of the Lord. This is commanded to those also who partake of the sacraments, that they examine their acts and thoughts and wash them with the tears of compunction. "For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself."
04_interl4613: of principal mortification, namely, which is done with pure intention for God alone; whence: "My hands dropped with myrrh" etc.
04_marg1707: TAKE SPICES OF PRINCIPAL MYRRH etc. STRABO. Zmyrna in Greek, in Latin is called myrrh, which is a tree in Arabia of five cubits, whose shoots the Arabs burn, that they may sprout and bear fruit better. From whose fumes they would contract incurable diseases, did they not counter them with the smoke of storax. The gum of this tree is properly called stacte, by misuse also myrrh.
04_interl4614: which is of ashen colour, and signifies the humility by which we understand that we are ash and shall return into ash. Cinnamon is a shrub, and grows in India or Ethiopia, only two cubits high. And it is called cinnamon because in the manner of a cane it has slender and folded stalks of ashen or black colour, which when broken give off a visible breath; and the slender is dear, but the thick cheap and despised. Calamus is an aromatic kind near Libanus.
04_interl4615: this grows in watery places, and grows to a great size, and gives a good odour; and it signifies faith, which grows through baptism
04_marg1708: OF MYRRH, CINNAMON, CALAMUS, CASSIA etc. These four kinds signify the four principal virtues, by which, with the oil of unction and the grace of God's mercy, the Church is to be dedicated and sanctified.
04_interl4616: let the measure be just and right
04_interl4617: because all things are to be done according to the rule of the Church
04_interl4619: the chrism with which the tabernacle is anointed, namely the faithful people of the Church, that is, those in whom the Godhead dwells as in a tabernacle. By the ointment also can be understood the virtues of the saints, or the odour of justice spread far and wide.
04_interl4620: All these have been set out above.
04_marg1709: AND THEY SHALL BE MOST HOLY etc. AUGUSTINE. When, namely, they have been anointed. What difference then will there be from those inner things which are covered by the veil?
04_marg1710: The like was said above of the altar of sacrifices, which is to be so understood that the people might touch the tabernacle when they offered victims or any gifts, and by touching were sanctified because of that oil with which all things were anointed: not as the priests, who were also anointed with it that they might perform the priesthood.
04_interl4621: because these things do not befit those who love the pleasure of the flesh
04_interl4624: because holy things are not to be given to dogs
04_interl4625: to a heretic or gentile or Jew
04_interl4626: from the company of the saints, to which he ought to be joined

04_marg1716: AND THOU SHALT MAKE INCENSE etc. GREGORY. We make incense compounded of spices when on the altar of good work we give off the odour of a multitude of virtues; which is made mixed and pure, because the more virtue is joined to virtue, the more purely is the incense of good odour shown forth. Whence it well follows: And when thou hast beaten all into very small powder, thou shalt set of it before the tabernacle of the testimony. We grind spices into very small powder when we pound our good works as in the mortar of the heart with hidden examination, and go over them minutely, that they may be truly good. To reduce spices to powder therefore is to grind the virtues by thinking them over, and to go over them to the fineness of hidden examination. And it is to be noted that of the same powder it is said: Thou shalt set of it before the tabernacle of the testimony, because our good things truly please in the sight of the judge when the mind grinds them by thinking more finely, and as it were makes powder of the spices, lest the good that is done be coarse and hard; which, unless going over it breaks it small, does not scatter its odour more finely.
04_marg1717: The incense, which is compounded of four most fragrant kinds ground to the greatest fineness, that is, stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense, signifies the prayers of the faithful; although these four seem to signify the four elements, so that frankincense, which is clear, may be compared to the air, stacte to the waters, galbanum and onyx to earth and fire; that through these the incense of all things which are in heaven and beneath heaven, and on earth, and in the waters, may be pleasing to God.

04_marg1729: LET ME ALONE etc. GREGORY. What is it to say to a servant: Let me alone, but to give him boldness to pray? As if to say: Weigh how much thou availest with me, and know that thou canst obtain whatever thou prayest for the people. In Job, however, it is said: "God, whose wrath no man can resist", whereas Moses resisted the wrath of God, who restrained the onset of the stroke from above by offering his own death, saying: Forgive this trespass, or else strike me out of thy book which thou hast written. Aaron too tempered the fire of the divine punishment with the smoke of incense; and Phinees, slaying those who were wanton with strangers, offered his zeal to the divine indignation and appeased the fury with the sword; David, offering himself to the smiting angel, obtained the grace of appeasement before the time set. But the wrath of God cannot be resisted when it moves itself (so to speak) from the marrow, nor does anyone's entreaty set itself against it profitably when God has once disposed something in anger from his inmost being. Hence it is that Moses, who wiped away the guilt of the whole people by his prayers and appeased the force of the divine anger, coming to the rock of Horeb and distrusting about the giving of water, could not enter the land of promise, the Lord being angry; and he afflicts himself over this matter and is troubled with desire, and could not drive from himself the anger of the vengeance disposed, he who, God willing, had removed it from the people. Hence David, the people being laid low, restrained by prayer the sword of the angel, whereas before, weeping and wailing, with bare feet, he mourned his son, and until he received in full the vengeance of the crime committed could not temper the wrath of God for himself.
04_marg1730: It can edify the reader according to the history if he weighs how in good rulers the authority of ruling and the kindness of consoling are mingled. For discipline or mercy is much forsaken if one be held without the other. But toward their subjects there ought to be in doctors or rulers both justly consoling mercy and piously severe discipline. For see Moses piously loving and strictly severe. For when it was said: "Go down: thy people hath sinned", as if to say: He who has fallen into such a sin is no longer mine; and it was added: Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them etc., often setting himself against the wrath of God he says: Either forgive them this trespass, or strike me out of thy book. Let us weigh with what bowels he loved the people, for whose life he asked to be struck out; and with how great zeal for righteousness, when he had obtained pardon, coming to the people, he says: "Put every man his sword upon his thigh" etc. See, he who asked the life of all with his own death extinguished the life of a few with the sword; within he burned with the fires of love, without he was kindled with the zeal of severity. So he loved those over whom he was set that he did not spare himself for them; so he pursued the offenders that he laid them low even when the Lord spared them; a strong envoy on both sides, he pleaded the cause of the people with God by prayers, the cause of God with the people by swords. Loving within, he withstood the divine wrath by supplicating; severe without, he consumed the fault by striking. He succoured all the more quickly in the punishment of a few. But God heard him the more quickly pleading for the people because he saw what he was about to do against the people for God. In ruling the people therefore Moses mingled both, that neither discipline should be lacking to mercy nor mercy to discipline.

04_marg1734: It is asked why the tables which the Lord wrote and made were broken, but those which were hewn by the hand of man lasted. But in this it is signified that God adorned the first man with reason and wit. He gave a wise and understanding heart, that he might know and fulfil without difficulty and error. By doing this therefore he as it were wrote and hewed certain tables; but man broke them when he gave in to the devil and made himself unworthy of that grace. He is commanded therefore to hew tables again, that is, to prepare the breadth of the heart to receive the commandments of God; and because he so violated free will that he can no longer do good of himself without the grace of God, let him strive to labour toward the virtues: for Adam was overcome in delights; Job overcame the devil on the dunghill.

04_marg1735: AND LAYING HOLD OF THE CALF etc. ISIDORE. In the calf the body of the devil is signified, that is, men in all nations, for whom the devil is the head, that is, the author, of these sacrileges. A golden calf, because the rites of idolatry seem to have been instructed by the wise, of whom it is said: Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools; and they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man etc.; and by such wisdom this golden calf, as it were, as even the wise men of the Egyptians were wont to adore figments. In the calf therefore is signified the whole body of the devil, that is, the whole fellowship of gentiles given to idolatry; this sacrilegious fellowship Christ burnt with the fire of which he says: "I am come to cast fire on the earth" etc. And elsewhere: There is no one that can hide himself from his heat; while the gentiles believe in him, the devilish form is melted by the fire of his power. Then the body is broken small, that is, scattered from that gathering of wicked conspiracy, it is humbled by the word of truth; and, broken small, it is cast into water, that the Israelites, that is, the preachers of the Gospel, may carry them over from baptism into their members, that is, into the Lord's body. Whence it is said to Peter: Kill and eat, when it could likewise have been said 'cut up and drink'; so the calf, by the fire of zeal and the edge of the word and the water of baptism, was swallowed up rather by those whom it was trying to swallow.

04_marg1740: PUT EVERY MAN HIS SWORD etc. GREGORY. To put the sword upon the thigh is to set the zeal of preaching before the pleasures of the flesh, so that when one strives to speak holy things, he must take care to tame suggestions. To go from gate to gate is to run about rebuking from vice to vice, through which fault enters the mind. To pass through the midst of the camp is to live within the Church with such evenness that he who reproves the faults of offenders does not rest in the favour of anyone. Whence it is added: Let every man kill his brother, and friend, and neighbour. He kills these who, when he finds things to be punished, spares from the sword of rebuke not even those whom he loves by kinship of the flesh. If therefore he is called God's who is stirred up by the zeal of divine love to strike vices, surely he denies that he is God's who refuses to rebuke the life of the carnal as much as is needful.

04_marg1741: AND THEY HAVE MADE TO THEMSELVES GODS etc. AUGUSTINE. He put the plural for the singular, as there: "These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt." But this manner of speech is not found except where it can also be said or understood of several. For it is not that, because the calf was one, several could not therefore be made, or that it was not therefore like many idols. By this manner of speech it was said that the thieves reviled the Lord, though Scripture testifies that one did this; but he was not the only thief. Nay more, when this manner of speech is made with proper names (in which way we have not yet found it made in the divine Scriptures), several are understood there, as some have said Phedras and Medeas, though there was one Phedra and one Medea, but they called Phedras and Medeas all who were like Phedra and Medea. So not without cause, nor at random as is done faultily by the unskilled, but in a certain manner and by certain rules are these manners of speech put in.

04_marg1743: AUGUSTINE. It is asked, since above Aaron was said to have stripped the people, why vengeance was not taken on him, neither when Moses commanded that every one the armed men met from gate to gate should be killed, nor afterward when the Lord struck the people for the making of the calf which Aaron had made; and it was not said 'which they made', but which Aaron made; and yet Aaron was not struck. Nay more, that which God commanded about his priesthood before the sin was fulfilled; but he commanded him and his sons to be washed, and so they were ordained in the priesthood. So he knows whom he spares until a change for the better; and whom he spares for a time, although he has foreknown that he will not be changed for the better; and whom he does not spare, that he may be changed for the better; and whom he does not spare so as not even to await his change. For "his judgments are incomprehensible, and his ways unsearchable".
04_marg1744: GO, GET THEE UP FROM THIS PLACE, THOU AND THY PEOPLE etc. AUGUSTINE. God, being angry, seems to say: Thou and thy people which thou hast brought out; otherwise he would have said: Thou and my people which I brought out. But when they demanded the idol, they spoke thus: This Moses, the man that brought us out of the land of Egypt etc.; and because they set their deliverance in a man, this is turned back on them when it is said: Thou and thy people which thou hast brought out of the land of Egypt; which is a charge against them, not against Moses. For Moses wished them to put their hope in the Lord, and to know that they were freed from that bondage by his mercy; and yet there was in him so great merit through the grace of God that he said to him: Let me alone, that I may be angry against them. But whether it be of one commanding, when he says: Let me alone, or as of one asking, either seems absurd. For if God commanded, the servant disobediently did not obey; and it was not fitting for God to ask this of a servant as a favour, since he could crush them even against his will. By these words therefore God signifies that it profited that people very much with him to be so loved by that man; that in this way we might be admonished, when our merits weigh us down so that we are not loved by God, that we can be relieved with him by the merits of those whom he truly loves. For when it is said by God to a man: Let me alone, and I will crush them, this is: I would crush them were they not loved by thee; as if to say: Do not love them, and I will crush them, because thy love intercedes that I may not do it. The Lord would have to be obeyed when he says: Do not love them, if he had said this commanding, and not rather admonishing and expressing what was calling him back from their punishment: and yet, even with him interceding, he does not leave the people without the scourge of discipline. For I know not how, so that Moses himself might so love them, God loved them more hiddenly, who terrified them with open voice.

04_marg1746: GO, GET THEE UP etc. AUGUSTINE. At once, as though he were still speaking to Moses himself, by a hidden turning, which in Greek is called apostrophe, he says to the people: I will send my angel before thee etc. A great and wonderful depth of sacrament: as though an angel could have greater mercy than the Lord, so as to spare a stiffnecked people; and yet through an angel, he himself being as it were absent, who can be absent nowhere, he says he will fulfil what he swore to their fathers; as though here too showing that he does this because he promised to the fathers, not because these were worthy. What then does it signify, unless perhaps that he is therefore not with those who are stiffnecked, because only humility and piety receive him as propitious and saving? And for God to be with stiffnecked men is nothing else than to be present avenging and punishing. Whence: "Turn away thy face from my sins", because if he turns toward, he overturns. For as wax melteth before the fire, so let the sinners perish at the presence of the Lord.

04_marg1748: AND WHEN MOSES WENT FORTH etc. GREGORY. The Hebrew people, freed from Egyptian bondage, when they saw the pillar of cloud as God spoke, stood each at the doors of his tabernacle and adored. Whence it is said: "And when Moses went forth to the tabernacle, all the people rose up, and every one stood in the door of his tabernacle." For what is it for the people to behold the pillar of cloud, and to stand at the doors of their tabernacles and adore, but that when the human mind beholds those higher and heavenly things in some manner in a dark way, it already goes out of the enclosure of the bodily dwelling by lifted thought, and humbly adores him whom, if it cannot see, it yet already wonders at his power through the enlightening of the spirit? And when Moses enters the tabernacle, the people behold his back and stand at the door of their pavilions, because when the preacher speaks lofty things of God, he already enters in some manner the tabernacle of the dwelling above; the office and power of whose preaching, if the weak cannot fully weigh, they yet as it were behold his back, because they follow by understanding the last things they are able; but in those very least things which they can grasp, they already as it were go out of their pavilions and stand at the doors, because they strive to leave the dwellings of the flesh and go forward to those joys of eternal life of which they hear.
04_marg1749: AND THEY BEHELD THE BACK etc. STRABO. Moses holds the figure of the law. The Jewish people therefore beheld the back of Moses, because it would understand nothing mystical, nothing spiritual in the law, but only the surface of the letter. Therefore his face was hidden, that is, the true and pure knowledge. When he had entered the tabernacle, the pillar of cloud came down and stood at the door. Another translation says that when Moses wished to enter the tabernacle, the cloud set itself before him and prevented him. But here it is said that when he had entered, the cloud spoke with him before the door. It is to be known therefore that he entered some part, namely the court, and then, before he entered the tabernacle, the cloud set itself in the way: in this place therefore it signifies those who are less perfect in knowledge and work and cannot penetrate the inner things of the Scriptures. But elsewhere, when he entered the midst of the cloud, he held the figure of the perfect, namely those who search out the secrets of the mystical senses.

04_marg1751: IF THEREFORE I HAVE FOUND FAVOUR etc. AUGUSTINE. By these words Moses shows that he did not see God with that familiar sight he desired, because all those visions of God which were offered to the sight of mortals, and from which came a sound by which mortal hearing might be reached, were shown forth by things assumed, as God willed, in the form he willed, so that in them the divine nature itself was perceived by no bodily sense, which is invisible, everywhere whole, and contained in no place. And because on two precepts, namely the love of God and of neighbour, the whole Law depends, therefore Moses showed his desire in both: in the love of God, where he says: If I have found favour in thy sight, shew me thyself etc.; in the love of neighbour, where he says: And that I may know that this nation is thy people etc.
04_marg1752: It was said before: Thou hast found favour in my sight; again he asks that he may find favour. For one grace does not suffice the saints. 04_marg1753: AND THEE I HAVE KNOWN etc. AUGUSTINE. Because I know thee above all etc. Does God know some more and some less? Or is it according to what is said to some in the Gospel: I know you not? It is according to another knowledge of God, by which God is said to know the things that please him and not to know the things that displease him, not because he is ignorant of them but because he does not approve them; as an art is rightly said not to know faults, since it disapproves them; and God knew Moses above all because Moses pleased God above all. It is to be noted that Moses himself had said to God before: Thou hast said to me: I know thee above all; which God is read to have said to him after he himself said this. But before, it is not read; that we may understand that not all things are written which God spoke with him; but it must be sought more carefully in the earlier parts of Scripture whether it is truly so.

04_marg1754: When Moses had said to the Lord: Shew me thy glory, he answered: I will pass before thee in my glory etc. Whereas a little before he himself had said: I will go before thee, and will give thee rest; which Moses seems to have taken thus: I will go before thee, as though he would not be present with the people on the way; and therefore he said: If thou thyself dost not come with us, bring me not out of this place etc. But God did not deny him this either, saying: This word also which thou hast spoken will I do. How then, when Moses had said to him: Shew me thy glory, does he seem to say again, as about to go before and not to be together with them: I will pass before thee, unless because this is something else? For he is understood to say: I will pass before thee, of whom it is said: When the hour was come that Jesus should pass out of this world to the Father etc. Which passing is called the Pasch; he passes before all the saints from this world to the Father, to prepare the mansions which he will give them in the resurrection of the dead, because, about to pass before all, he was made the firstborn from the dead. And he greatly commends his grace when he says: And I will proclaim in the name of the Lord in thy sight, as in the sight of the people of Israel. Moses, when he heard these things, signified the people. For in the sight of that nation, scattered everywhere, the Lord Christ is proclaimed among all the gentiles.

04_interl4760: The mercy of God is free and spontaneous to all. For when he has mercy it is grace; when he permits hardening it is just judgment, though hidden.
04_marg1756: AND I WILL HAVE MERCY etc. AUGUSTINE. What he added: And I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I have shown mercy, shows more expressly the calling by which he called us into his kingdom and his glory, not for our merits but for his mercy. For since he promised that he would bring in the gentiles, saying: I will proclaim in the name of the Lord in thy sight, he commends that he does this mercifully. Whence: "For I say that Christ Jesus was minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers. But that the Gentiles" etc. This therefore was foretold: I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy etc. By which words he forbade man to glory as of the merits of his own virtues, that "he that glorieth may glory in the Lord". For he does not say: I will have mercy on such or such, but on whom I shall have been merciful, that he may show that no one has deserved the mercy of so great a calling by preceding works or merits. For Christ died for the ungodly. But whether he wished to repeat the same thing when he added: I will show mercy to whom I have shown mercy, or, as others have translated: to whom I shall be merciful, or whether there is some difference, I know not. For by this repetition God can show the firmness of his mercy, as it is said: Amen, Amen; and: So be it, so be it; and the repetition of Pharao's dream, and many like things; or that in both peoples, that is, the Gentiles and the Hebrews, God so foretold that he would show mercy.

04_marg1757: THOU CANST NOT SEE etc. AUGUSTINE. After the commendation of his mercy he answers what had been said to him: Shew me thy glory, or Shew me thyself. Thou canst not, he says, see my face. For man shall not see my face and live; showing that God as he is cannot appear to this life of corruptible flesh, that is, be seen as he is. For in that life he can, where, that one may live, one must die to this life.
04_marg1758: FOR MAN SHALL NOT SEE etc. GREGORY. John also says: "No man hath seen God at any time." For as long as one lives mortally here, God can be seen through certain images, but cannot through the very form of his nature. Hence it is that Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as a man is wont to speak with his friend, says: If I have found favour in thy sight, shew me thyself openly. For if he with whom he spoke were not God, he would say 'shew me God', and not 'shew thyself'. But if he was God, why did he ask to see him whom he saw? But he thirsted to behold through the brightness of his uncircumscribed nature him whom he had already begun to see through certain images. The fathers of the Old Testament therefore saw God, and yet "no man hath seen God at any time", because to those living in this flesh he could be seen through certain circumscribed images, and could not be seen through the uncircumscribed light of eternity. But if to some living in this flesh, yet growing with inestimable virtue, the brightness of the eternal God can be seen by the keenness of contemplation, yet man shall not see him and live, because he who sees the wisdom which is God dies utterly to this life, lest he be held by love of it. But there have been some who said that even in that region of beatitude God is beheld in his brightness but not seen in his nature. But he himself promises to those who love him, saying: "He that loveth me shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him." As if to say: You who behold me in your nature, it remains that you see me in my nature. And elsewhere: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." Hence Paul says: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner: but then face to face" etc. But because Peter says: "On whom the angels desire to look", there are some who suppose that not even the angels see God, whereas the Lord said: Their angels always see the face of my Father; but the angels both see God and desire to see him. For if they so desire to see that they do not enjoy their desire, desire without fruit has anxiety, and anxiety punishment. But the angels are strangers to all punishment, because punishment and beatitude never agree. Again, when we say that they are satisfied with the vision of God, according to that: "I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear", it is to be considered that loathing is wont to follow satiety. But lest there be anxiety in desire, they are satisfied while desiring; and lest there be loathing in satiety, being satisfied they desire; they desire therefore without labour, because satiety accompanies desire, and they are satisfied without loathing, because satiety is ever kindled from desire.

04_marg1759: BEHOLD, HE SAID, A PLACE etc. AUGUSTINE. Again, with a clause put between, Scripture saying, And the Lord said, there follows: Behold a place with me. What place is not with God, who is absent nowhere? But signifying the Church, as commending it as his temple: And thou shalt stand, he says, upon the rock. Because upon this rock, says the Lord, I will build my Church; as soon as my glory shall pass, thou shalt stand, namely, upon the rock; because after the passing of Christ, that is, his passion and resurrection, the faithful people stood upon the rock.
04_marg1760: There is a place with me etc. The place is the Church, the rock the Lord, Moses the Jewish people, which did not believe when the Lord preached on earth. It therefore stood on the rock beholding the back of the Lord as he passed, because namely after the Lord's passion and ascension, brought into the Church by faith, it deserved to perceive Christ, and knew the back parts of him whose presence it did not see.
04_marg1761: There is a place with me etc. The Church, namely, from which alone truth is beheld, sacrifice is received; it alone intercedes for those who err. Whence it is commanded of the victim of the lamb: In one house shall you eat it, neither shall you carry forth of the flesh thereof out of the house; because in the one catholic Church the true victim of the Redeemer is sacrificed, and the holy thing is not given to dogs. It alone is that in which good work is done fruitfully. Whence also only those who laboured within the vineyard received the reward of the penny. It alone is that which guards those set within it with the strong bond of charity. Whence the water of the flood raised the ark indeed to higher places, but all whom it found outside the ark it destroyed.

04_marg1763: AUGUSTINE. And I will cover thee with my hand until I pass, and I will take away my hand, and then thou shalt see my back parts better; but my face shall not be seen by thee. Whereas he had said: Thou shalt stand upon the rock as soon as my glory shall pass, where he is understood to have promised his own firmness on the rock after his passing, how is what he says to be taken: I will set thee in the cleft of the rock, and I will cover thee with my hand until I pass, and I will take away my hand, and then thou shalt see my back parts; as though, he being already set on the rock, he covers him with his hand and then passes, whereas he cannot be on the rock except after his passing? But a recapitulation of a thing passed over is to be understood, which Scripture often uses. For afterward he said what is first in the order of time, which runs thus: I will cover thee with my hand until I pass, and then thou shalt see my back parts. For my face shall not be seen by thee; and thou shalt stand upon the rock as soon as my glory shall pass, and I will set thee in the cleft of the rock. For this was done in those whom Moses then signified, that is, in the Israelites who afterward believed in Christ, that is, as soon as his glory passed; because when he had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, and, the Spirit being sent, the Apostles spoke with all tongues, many of those who had crucified Christ were pricked to the heart. For blindness in part has happened in Israel, as had been said: I will cover thee with my hand until I pass. Whence: Thy hand was heavy upon me by day, namely when Christ did divine miracles; by night, when as man he died. But afterward, pricked in heart, they said: What shall we do? And they were bidden by the Apostles to do justice and to do penance; but before they were blinded, so that they did not know. "For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." That this too was a prophecy the thing itself shows, because of the rock or its cleft, of the laying on of the hand and the sight of the back parts, nothing is read to have followed in visible deed. For at once Scripture adds: And the Lord said to Moses, while he was still speaking the things above; then it joins on what the Lord says afterward: Hew thee two tables of stone etc.

04_marg1764: WHO RENDEREST THE INIQUITY etc. GREGORY. Since it is written: What is it that you use among you this parable as a proverb in the land of Israel, saying: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord, this parable shall be no more to you a proverb in Israel: as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, the same shall die; what is it that is said: Who renderest the iniquity of the fathers to the children and to the grandchildren? We draw original sin from our fathers, and unless we are saved through the grace of baptism we bear even the guilt of our parents, because we are still one with them. He renders the iniquity of the fathers on the children when for the fault of the parent the soul of the offspring is polluted by original sin. And again he does not render the iniquity of the fathers on the children, because when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we have no longer the faults of our parents but those we ourselves commit. Otherwise: he who imitates the iniquity of a wicked parent is bound also by his offence; but he who does not imitate it is not weighed down by his offence. Whence it comes about that the wicked son of a wicked father pays not only his own sins which he adds, but also his father's, when, not ignorant of God's anger, he does not fear to add his own malice. And it is just that he who does not fear, under a strict judge, to imitate the ways of a wicked father, should be compelled also to pay for his faults. Whence: The soul of the father is mine, the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, the same shall die; because sometimes sons perish even from a father's sin. But when original sin is blotted out, they are not held in soul by the wickedness of their parents. For why is it that little children are often seized by demons, but that the flesh of the son is punished by the father's penalty? For the wicked father is struck in himself and despises it. He strikes him therefore in his children, that he may be sharply burned, and the father's pain is rendered through the flesh of the children, that by the children's punishment the father's wicked mind may be punished. But when not little children but sons already grown are struck even for their parents' fault, they pay the penalties of those whose deeds they have followed. Whence it is rightly said: Unto the third and fourth generation; because up to that generation, which the sons imitate, they can see the life of their parents; the vengeance extends to those who have seen what they wickedly followed.

04_marg1772: AND HE WROTE UPON THE TABLES etc. AUGUSTINE. It is said of Moses that he himself wrote, to whom God also said a little before: "Write thee these words." But when he first received the Law, whose tables he cast down and broke, he was neither said to have hewn them, nor was he told to write, nor is he related to have written them, as it is now said: He wrote upon the tables the words of the testament etc.; but then it was said: And he gave to Moses, as soon as he had ceased to speak to him in mount Sinai, two tables of testimony, tables of stone written with the finger of God; and a little after: And Moses returned, he says, and came down from the mount, and the two tables, and the tables were the work of God, and the writing of God was graven in the tables. A great question arises how those tables which Moses was, the Lord foreknowing it, to break, are said to be not the work of man but of God, and not written by man but by the finger of God; but the later ones, which were to last long and to be in the tabernacle and in the temple of God, were by God's command hewn and written by man. Was the grace of God signified in the former, not the work of man, of which they were made unworthy, turning back in heart to Egypt and making an idol, whence they were deprived of that benefit, and therefore Moses broke the tables? But by these later ones are signified those who glory in their own works. Whence the Apostle: For they, not knowing the justice of God, and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to the justice of God; and therefore the tables were written by human work, which remained with them, signifying the same men who would glory in their own works, not in the finger of God, that is, in the Spirit of God. Certainly then the repetition of the Law signifies the New Testament. But that one signified the Old, whence it was broken and abolished. Especially because when the Law is given the second time it is given with no terror, as that was, amid the din of fires, clouds and trumpets. Whence the people, terrified, say: Let not the Lord speak to us, lest we die. Whence it is signified that there is fear in the Old Testament, love in the New. How then is this question solved, why those were the work of God, these the work of man, and those written by the finger of God, these written by man? Or perhaps is the Old Testament rather signified in the former for this reason, that God there commanded, but man did not do? For "the Law" was set in the Old Testament to convict transgressors, which "entered in that sin might abound". For it was not fulfilled by fear, since it is not fulfilled except by charity. And therefore it is called the work of God, because God established the Law, God wrote it: not the work of man, because man did not obey God, and the Law rather made him guilty. But in the second tables man made the tables through the help of God. Whence the Lord says: I am not come to destroy the Law, but to fulfil. And the Apostle: Love is the fulfilling of the Law. That therefore was made easy for man in the New Testament which in the Old was hard, for him who has the faith that worketh by charity, that finger of God, that is, the Spirit of God, writing it within in the heart, not outside on stone. Whence: "Not in tables of stone, but in the fleshly tables of the heart"; since "the charity of God", by which the precept is truly fulfilled, "is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us". This then is the Law first given, where the Old Testament is signified, which is the work of God only, and written by the finger of God. Whence the Apostle says: "Wherefore the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good." The Law therefore, holy and good, is the work of God: where man does nothing, because he does not obey, but is rather weighed down by guilt, the Law threatening and condemning. But man is blessed when this "holy and just and good commandment" is also his work, but through the grace of God.

04_marg1773: ISIDORE. Moses goes up again into the mount, and again God gives him the law on other tables hewn after the pattern of the former. But those which he first received he broke without delay, which bore the image of the ancient Law, which ceased after no long interval because of the people's sin. But those hewn after the pattern of the former signified the New Testament; which were not broken, because the New Testament remains for ever; whence they are fittingly marked by ten words, that by that number the figure of the cross may be expressed, which ten signifies, being formed in the shape of a cross. For Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, namely through the passion of the cross, whose image was on the tables.
04_marg1774: As Moses comes down with the tables, his face is seen glorified, but yet it is covered with a veil; in which it signified that the law was covered with a mystic veil and hidden from unbelievers. For the word of the law has the knowledge of glory, but secret; it has also the horns of the two Testaments, with which it goes armed against the doctrines of falsehood. For when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart; and plainly, while unbelievers take the Scripture of the law and the prophets carnally, the whole face of Moses is covered with a kind of veil, so that they cannot bear the glory of the law as it speaks; but if they be turned to God, the veil shall be taken away; the killing letter will die, the quickening spirit will be quickened. For the Lord is a Spirit, and the law is spiritual. Whence: "Open thou my eyes: and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law."
