04_marg1775: AND AARON AND THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL SEEING etc. ORIGEN. It is written that Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, and his face was glorified, and the colour of his countenance, and they feared to come to him. And after a little Moses put a veil upon his face. But when he went in before the Lord to speak to him, he took away the veil. Setting this out the Apostle says: Now if the ministration of death, engraven with letters upon stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not steadfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance, which is made void: how shall not the ministration of the Spirit be rather in glory? And a little after: And not as Moses put a veil upon his face, that the children of Israel might not steadfastly look on the face of his countenance. For their senses were made dull etc. Who would not be afraid of the mark of a dull heart? The face of Moses is glorified, but the children of Israel cannot steadfastly look on his face. The people of the Synagogue cannot steadfastly look. But if anyone has a life more eminent than the crowd, he can. For now too the veil is set on the reading of the Old Testament, and Moses speaks with glorified countenance. But we cannot gaze on the glory, because we are still the people, and have nothing more of zeal, nothing more of merit, than the rest of the common folk. But when anyone shall be turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away. Our turning therefore is the cause of the veil's being taken away. While therefore, reading the divine Scriptures, we do not understand, while they are obscure and shut, we are not yet turned. For to those turned, the veil will at once be taken away. Everyone who, when the words of the law are recited, is occupied with common tales, is turned away; and he who is anxious about the business of the world, about money, about gains, about the cares of possessions and the desire of riches, who strives after the glory of the world and the honours of the age, is turned away. He too who seems a stranger to these, but stands and hears the words of the Law intent with face and eyes, yet wanders in heart and thought, is turned away. What then is it to be turned? If we turn our backs on all these things, and give ourselves to the word of God with zeal, acts, mind and care. For let us meditate on the law day and night, and, leaving all, give ourselves to God and be exercised in his testimonies; this is to be turned to the Lord. But which of us seeks the divine writings with as great labour and zeal as he sought human ones? Some, as soon as they have heard what is read recited, go away at once. There is no inquiry with one another about the things that have been read, no conferring. They do not ask their fathers to tell them, nor the priests to declare to them. Others do not even wait patiently until the lessons are recited in church; others do not even know if they are recited, but in the remoter places of the church are occupied with worldly tales: on whom there is no longer a veil upon the heart, but a wall and rampart is set. For if he who is present, hears, attends, and goes over and discusses what he hears, asks and learns, can scarcely come to the freedom of knowledge, he "who stoppeth his ears lest he hear", and turns his back to the face of the reader, how is he to be said to have a veil laid upon his heart, to whom not even the very veil of the letter by which the sense is veiled, which is the sound of the voice, has come? The face of Moses therefore is made glorious: for the things he speaks have glory, but it is covered and hidden, and "all his glory is within".
04_marg1776: Consider this too, that in the law the countenance of Moses is glorified, though it is covered with a veil. But his hand, put into his bosom, became leprous. In which the form of the whole Law seems to me to be most fully marked out. For in the countenance the word of the law, in the hand the works are signified. Because therefore no one was to be justified by the works of the law, nor could the law lead anyone to perfection, the hand becomes leprous and is hidden in the bosom, as having nothing of perfect work. The face therefore is glorified, but covered with a veil, because its word has the glory of knowledge, but hidden. Whence: "The uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me." The face of Moses therefore has glory, the hand disgrace. Lastly he is commanded to loose his shoe, so that there was no glory in his feet, although this was done not without mystery. For the feet are the last part of man. It was shown therefore that in the last times Moses would loose his shoe, that another might take the bride, and she would be called "the house of the unshod" until the present. Moses therefore has nothing glorious in the law but his face alone. But in the gospel he is glorified wholly. Whence: There appeared Moses and Elias in glory, speaking with him. Here it is not said that his countenance was glorified, but that he appeared wholly in glory speaking with Jesus, where is fulfilled what was promised him on mount Sina: Thou shalt see my back parts. For he saw the things that were done in the latter days and rejoiced, because he not only came down from the mount glorified in countenance, but went up from the mount glorified wholly; and he saw now present him of whom he had said: The Lord your God will raise up to you a prophet of your brethren, like unto me etc., and making good his words. And lest he should hesitate in anything, he hears the Father saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye him." Moses said: Him you shall hear; the Father, saying: "Hear ye him", shows him present. Moses also rejoices, because he too in a manner lays down the veil, turned to the Lord, when what he foretold is evidently fulfilled, or when the time has come for the things he had covered to be revealed through the Spirit. But let us see what the Apostle says: "Now the Lord is a Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." I think that the Word of God, according to what profits the hearers, is named now the way, now the truth, now the life, now the resurrection, now also flesh, and now Spirit. For although he truly received the substance of flesh from the virgin, in which he bore the cross and began the resurrection, yet the Apostle says: And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him so no longer: because therefore now his word calls us to a subtler understanding, and wishes us to perceive nothing carnal in the law, he says that he who wishes to take away the veil should turn to the Lord, not as to flesh but as to spirit, that he may come from carnal things to spiritual, and from bondage to liberty, for "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty". But elsewhere he says: I judged not myself to know anything among you, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified. To these he did not say that the Lord is a Spirit, and the wisdom of God, because they could not know Christ according as he is wisdom, but according as he was crucified. But those to whom he said: We speak wisdom among the perfect, not of this world, but the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, did not need the Word of God according as "the Word was made flesh", but according as he is wisdom hidden in a mystery. To those therefore who are called to spiritual understanding it is said: "Now the Lord is a Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty": by which, namely, turned to the Lord and freed from the bondage of the world, we may seek the liberty of knowledge.
04_marg1777: AND THEN HE SPOKE etc. AUGUSTINE. After Moses came down from the mount, the works of building the tabernacle and of the priestly vesture are commanded; before giving any command about the making of these, he spoke to the people about the keeping of the sabbath. Where it rightly moves us, since he had received the ten words of the Law on the tables which he himself hewed and wrote, why, after he came down, he admonished the people about the sabbath alone. For if, because of the same precepts of the Law, it was superfluous for the people to hear them again, why was not this also superfluous, since it is read among those same ten precepts? Or is this too like the veil with which he covered his face, because the children of Israel could not gaze on the brightness of his countenance? For of the ten precepts he commanded this alone to the people, which is said there to be figurative: for the other nine we do not doubt are to be kept in the New Testament as there. But that one about the sabbath was so far veiled and commanded in mystery that today it is not kept by us. But let us gaze only on what is signified. In that rest, where servile works are bidden to cease, great is the height of the grace of God. For good works are then done with rest when faith worketh by charity: but fear hath torment, and in torment what rest? Whence: "Fear is not in charity." But "charity is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us". Therefore the sabbath is a holy rest to the Lord: to be ascribed, namely, to the grace of God, not to us as from ourselves. Otherwise our works will be such that they are either human sins or done with fear, not with love; and therefore servile works without rest are everlasting. For not in vain was the sabbath of sabbaths instituted. Above, when God spoke first of the anointing of the tabernacle, he said that by the same unction all those things were sanctified and made holy of holies. But the altar of holocausts, sanctified by the same unction, he had said was made holy of the holy. And there seemed to be this difference, that he had called none of them holy of holies except what is separated from the holy only by the veil, namely where the ark of the testament and the altar of incense were. Now, when he repeated the same things, he said of the anointed tabernacle and the things that were in it that they were sanctified by that unction and made holy. But the altar of holocaust, which he had said before was made holy of the holy, he now said was made holy of holies by the same unction. Whence it is understood that holy of the holy and holy of holies are the same; and by this, that all those anointed things, that is, the whole tabernacle and whatever was in it, which he before called holy of holies, mean just as much as what he now calls holy: nor is each of them called after that unction only holy of the holy, but also holy of holies, like the altar of holocaust; so that now there is no difference, so far as this name is concerned, between the things that were within the veil, namely where the ark of the testimony was, and the rest that are outside, except that those were so called the holies of holies, or the holy of holies, that they were so called even before the unction; but the rest were sanctified by unction that they might receive this name.

04_marg1778: SET ASIDE WITH YOU etc. ORIGEN. Another reading: Take from among yourselves a redemption for the Lord. Let every one that has conceived in his heart offer firstfruits to the Lord. Moses does not wish you to offer to God anything that is outside you: From among yourselves, he says, take, and offer firstfruits to the Lord, as each has conceived in heart, gold, silver etc. The spiritual law requires gold for the tabernacle, and other materials which we have within us and can bring forth from ourselves. For Scripture says: The word is nigh, in thy mouth and in thy heart. For if thou confess the Lord Jesus, and believe in thy heart that God hath raised him up from the dead, thou shalt be saved. If therefore thou hast believed 'in thy heart', thy heart and thy understanding are the best gold. Thou hast therefore offered gold for the tabernacle, the faith of thy heart. If thou hast confessed, the word of confession is silver. These are within thee; these, even if thou art naked, thou canst have. And what he adds: Each as he has conceived in heart, looks to this. For thou wilt not be able to offer God anything of thy understanding or of thy word unless thou hast first conceived in heart the things that are written; unless thou hast been attentive and heard diligently, thy gold cannot be proved, nor thy silver. For it is required to be proved. Whence: "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire, purged from the earth, refined seven times." If therefore thou hast conceived in heart the things that are written, thy gold, that is, thy understanding, will be proved, and thy silver, that is, thy word, will be proved.
04_marg1779: You who are accustomed to be present at the divine mysteries know how, when you receive the body of the Lord, you keep it with caution and reverence, lest any little of it fall. For if it fall, you believe yourselves guilty, and rightly you believe it: how do you think it a lesser sin to have neglected the word of God than his body? They are commanded therefore to offer beginnings, that is, firstfruits. He who offers what is first necessarily has himself what remains. See how much he must abound in gold or silver and all the other things that are commanded, so that we may both offer to the Lord and have left over for ourselves. For first my understanding ought to understand God, and offer him the firstfruits of its understanding, that it may consequently know the rest; let the word also do this; all these things that are in us do it.
04_marg1780: LET EVERY ONE THAT IS WILLING etc. ORIGEN. Another reading: Let each of you, he says, as he has conceived in heart, offer firstfruits to the Lord. I ask what are the firstfruits of gold, or the firstfruits of silver? And how do firstfruits seem to be kept of fine linen, scarlet and purple? Or how is each to offer as he has conceived in heart? There are those who conceive in heart the things that are read. There are those who do not conceive at all, intent on the works of the world or the reckonings of gain. The women only chatter, make a din with tales, and do not allow silence to be; they think of their children, or of wool, or of household needs. They learn to go about from house to house, speaking not only wordily but curiously things which they ought not. How then do they conceive? No one conceives in heart but he who is free in heart, free in mind and wholly intent. Otherwise he cannot offer to God. And it is just that each be found to have his portion in the temple of the Lord. For it is not hidden from the Lord what each offers. How glorious for thee, if it be said in the temple of the Lord: This gold, with which the ark of the testament is covered, is his. The silver, of which the sockets and pillars are, is his; the brass of which the rings and the laver and certain parts of the pillars were made, or the stones of the ephod and the logion, or the purple with which the high priest is adorned, and the scarlet, are his; and every other thing one by one. How unseemly, how wretched, if the Lord, visiting the tabernacle, find nothing of thy gift, know nothing offered by thee. So undevout, so unfaithful hast thou lived, that thou hast placed nothing of remembrance of thee in the temple of the Lord. For as the prince of this world comes to each one seeking whether he may find anything of his acts in us, and, if he finds it, claims us for himself: so if the Lord, coming, find something of thine in his tabernacle, he defends thee as his and calls thee his own.
04_marg1781: ORIGEN. It seems to be put for fortitude; I think it can also be taken for the voice. For the word is one thing, the voice another. For a word is called speech supported by reason. But the voice is the same whether it be spoken in Latin or in Greek, whether loudly or softly. Whence: "I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." To speak with tongues therefore and to interpret from one tongue into another is the offering of brass. For it is necessary that the tabernacle of the Lord have all things, and that nothing be lacking in the house of God. The offering of brass therefore is the voice which turns another's sense into another tongue. But the word is that which brings forth one's own sense. Let all things therefore be offered to God: sense, word and voice.

04_marg1782: VIOLET, PURPLE etc. ORIGEN. Let us look at the rest: violet, purple, scarlet doubled, and fine twisted linen. These hold the figure of the four elements of which the world and the human body consist, that is, of air, fire, water, earth. Violet is referred to the air, which the colour itself shows; and scarlet to fire; purple to water, because it takes its juice from the waters; fine linen to the earth, from which it springs. We too therefore have all these things in ourselves, since we are bidden to offer firstfruits to the Lord from them. Therefore he says: Take from among yourselves, and you shall bring firstfruits to the Lord.
04_marg1783: AND SCARLET TWICE DYED etc. ORIGEN. Let us see why the scarlet is doubled. This colour indicates the element of fire, which has a twofold power: one by which it gives light, another by which it burns. This is the reason of the history. Mystically too fire is twofold. For there is fire in this world and in the world to come. The Lord says: "I am come to cast fire on the earth." This fire gives light. He will say in the future: Depart into everlasting fire etc. That fire burns. But this which he came to cast "enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world"; yet it has something which burns. Whence: Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he opened to us the Scriptures? But I know not whether that fire in the world to come, which burns, has anything that gives light. But let us see how we can offer this doubled fire. If thou art a doctor and buildest the tabernacle, that is, the Church of God, and it is said to thee: Behold, I have given my words in thy mouth as fire: if then, teaching and building the Church of God, thou dost only rebuke, reprove and chastise, and upbraid the sins of the people, but bringest forth nothing of consolation from the divine Scriptures, explainest nothing obscure, openest nothing of more sacred understanding, thou hast offered scarlet, but not doubled. For thy fire only burns, it does not give light. Again, if in teaching thou openest the mysteries of the Law and discussest its secrets, but dost not reprove the sinner, nor correct the negligent, nor hold the severity of discipline, thou hast offered scarlet, but not doubled. For thy fire only gives light, it does not kindle. He therefore who offers rightly and divides rightly offers scarlet doubled, so as to mingle with the light of knowledge a little fire of severity.
04_marg1784: If anyone worthily understands the going out of the Hebrews from Egypt, and the passing of the Red Sea, and all the way that is made through the desert, and each station of the camps, so as to receive also the law of God written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, and understands in these the increases of the virtues, and fulfils each in himself, he can come to the understanding of the tabernacle. Of which the Apostle says: For there was a tabernacle made the first, wherein was the candlestick, and the setting forth of loaves, which is called the Holy. And after the veil, the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of holies, having a golden censer, and the ark of the testament, and in it the two tables, and the manna, and the rod of Aaron that had blossomed. But what he adds: "Of which it is not now the time to speak particularly", some refer to that time in which he was writing to the Hebrews. Others think that because of the greatness of the mysteries he denies that the whole time of the present life is fit for it. But after his manner he opens a few things to many, that it may be shut to the negligent, but found by those who seek and opened to those who knock. Whence again he says: For Jesus is not entered into the holies made with hands, the patterns of the true: but into heaven itself, that he may appear now in the presence of God "through the veil, that is to say, his flesh". Since then he interpreted the veil of the inner tabernacle as the flesh of Christ, and the Holies themselves as heaven or the heavens, and Christ as the high priest who he says entered once into the Holies, having obtained eternal redemption: from these few things, if anyone knows how to understand the sense of Paul, he has opened to us a great sea of understanding. David too says: I shall go over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. And elsewhere: "Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle? or who shall rest in thy holy hill? He that walketh without blemish, and worketh justice." That is not the tabernacle which the prophet desires, made of skins and curtains and coverings of haircloth and the other materials of our use. For how is it true that no one dwells in this tabernacle but "the innocent in hands and clean of heart", when in the material tabernacle the worst priests, sons of pestilence, often dwelt, and the ark of the testament was taken and held by the Philistines? He therefore must be innocent in hands and clean of heart who dwells in the tabernacle which God pitched, and not man. The Lord also mentions not one tabernacle but several, and not temporal but eternal, saying: "That when you shall fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings." And the Apostle: Desiring to be clothed upon with our habitation that is from heaven. Follow therefore, leaving the earth, the prophetic and apostolic sense, and, what is greater, the word of Christ, that with all thy mind thou mayest ascend into heaven, and there seek the magnificence of the eternal dwelling or tabernacle, whose figure is shadowed forth on earth through Moses; to whom the Lord says: See, he says, that thou make all things according to the pattern which was shewn thee in the mount. The whole people therefore is commanded, each contributing according to his strength, to make the tabernacle, that all may in a manner be one tabernacle. And the contribution is made not of necessity but of free will: Thou shalt make, he says, a sanctification, and thence I will be seen by you. God therefore wishes us to make him a sanctification. For he promises that if we make him a sanctification he will be seen by us. Whence the Apostle: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see God. And he who has been sanctified in body and spirit, through purity of heart and body, will see God. Let us make therefore a sanctification for the Lord, all of us one, and each one one. For let us all make one, that is, the Church which is holy, "not having spot or wrinkle", but having for pillars, namely, its doctors and ministers, of whom it is said: Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me the right hands of fellowship, and to Barnabas. In the tabernacle the pillars are joined by bars put between them; in the churches the doctors are joined in fellowship by right hands given to one another. But these pillars are silvered, and their sockets. And two sockets are assigned to each pillar: one which is called the head and is set on top; the other which is truly called the socket and is put under the pillar as a foundation. Those pillars are silvered which preach the word of God and receive it through the Holy Ghost: "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire." And these preachers have the prophets for sockets. For they set the Church "upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets", using whose testimonies they confirm the faith of Christ. And the head of the pillars is he of whom the Apostle says: The head of the man is Christ. By the hangings, which are set in loops and hung from rings and tied with cords after the manner of curtains, stretched twenty-eight cubits in length and four cubits in breadth, is had the people of believers, which clings and hangs on the cords of faith. For a threefold cord is not broken, which is the faith of the Trinity, from which the Church hangs and is held up. And the measure of one court is stretched twenty-eight cubits in length and four in breadth, in which the law set into the four Gospels is marked. For seven signifies the law, which, when joined with four, four times seven make the number twenty-eight. These courts are ten, that they may hold the whole number of perfection and signify the decalogue of the law. And now the kinds of violet and fine linen and purple unfold many and divers works. Thence the hangings; thence the outer and inner veil; thence the whole vesture of the priest and high priest made of gold and gems, by which we can understand the kinds of virtues with which the Church is adorned. Faith is compared to gold, the word of preaching to silver; brass to patience; to incorruptible wood the knowledge which comes through the wood, or the incorruption of chastity which does not grow old; to fine linen virginity, to scarlet the glory of confession, to purple the brightness of chastity, to violet the hope of the kingdom of heaven. And what or of what sort are the vestments of the priests he declares, saying: "Let thy priests be clothed with justice" etc. And the Apostle: "Put ye on the bowels of mercy"; and he designates nobler vestments: Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh.
04_marg1785: In the building of the tabernacle, that the silver pillars might stand within, pins of brass were commanded to be made round about outside, by which the tabernacle might be held tied. Of which it is written: Thou shalt make the pins of the tabernacle and of the court with their little cords. The fathers of the Old Testament, who stood far off from the incarnation of Christ by intervals of time, seemed to be outside; but from the blood of Abel the passion of the Church began, and the Church of the elect who went before and who follow is one. But because it is said to the disciples: Many kings and prophets have desired to see the things that you see, and have not seen them, to have stood as it were outside, for the ancient fathers, is not to have seen bodily the presence of the Redeemer. They were outside therefore, but not divided from the Church, because in mind and in the work of preaching they held the loftiness of the Church, which we behold not by waiting for it but by having it. For as we are saved in the passion that is past, so they were saved by faith in the same passion to come. They therefore were outside, not outside the mystery, but outside the time. Whence in the building of the tabernacle, that the silver pillars might stand within, pins of brass were fixed outside round about, by which the tabernacle might be held tied, and cords were tied to the pins, that the tabernacle might remain fixed; because, that the apostles might stand firm in the light of their word, and the whole tabernacle, that is, the Church, might stand in the integrity of faith, the fathers of the Old Testament and the prophets were fixed outside like pins, that with the cords of their words they might bind faith to our minds, and this tabernacle of God might remain unshaken. They were therefore before the time of this Church, but yet they bind those who are in it, because while they preached the heavenly mysteries to come, after they were shown they made them credible to all. That the pillars therefore may stand immovable within, the pins hold the cords outside; because the preaching of those who could both see and preach it before it happened obtained that the holy apostles should perfectly believe the mystery of life. The pillars were made of silver, the pins of brass, because what the apostles clearly preach, this the prophets spoke obscurely under a mystical understanding. Rightly therefore are they marked by brass, because they were not clear in preaching. But the apostles, because they had the light of preaching in the mystery of the Redeemer, are expressed by silver pillars. And it is to be noted that silver sounds and shines, but brass sounds and does not shine; because the preachers of the New Testament spoke openly, and could also show the things they spoke of. But the preachers of the Old Testament, because they spoke obscure things of the heavenly mystery through the shadows of allegories, gave as it were a sound without light.
04_marg1786: After this the men took from their wives, all to whom it seemed good in mind, and brought gems and earrings and rings and hairpins and bracelets. These gifts too they offer to God who conceive understanding in heart, who have a mind given and intent to the word of God. And the men offer from their wives earrings and gems and bracelets. The woman is taken as the flesh, the man as the rational sense. Good are these women who obey their husbands; good is the flesh which no longer resists the spirit, but obeys and consents. Therefore if two or three of you shall agree concerning anything whatsoever you shall ask, it shall be done to you, says the Lord. They offer therefore earrings from their wives when hearing is offered to the Lord; and bracelets, that is, right works, good works, which are done through the flesh. These the rational sense offers to the Lord. And hairpins, he who knows well how to discern what is to be done, what avoided, what pleases God or what displeases, what is just, what unjust. These are the hairpins which they offer to God, because they are wise women, and they made whatever was needed for the vestments of the high priest. But those women who offered their earrings that the calf might be made were foolish, who turned away their hearing from the truth and turned it to fables and impiety; and therefore they offered their earrings that the head of the calf might be made. And in the book of Judges too we find an idol made from the earrings of women. Blessed therefore are these women, blessed the flesh, which offers to the Lord its earrings, bracelets and rings, and all the works of its hands which it does in the commandments of the Lord. And he with whom incorruptible wood was found offered it to the Lord. If anyone loves Christ in incorruption, he offers incorruptible wood to God. Blessed therefore is he with whom an incorrupt understanding or an incorrupt body is found, and offers this to God. Whence also he said well: He with whom incorruptible wood was found. Of gold he did not say, nor of silver, with whom it was found: for understanding and word can be found with all. Nor of the four colours: it belongs to all to consist of four elements according to the body. But incorruptible wood, that is, the grace of incorruption and virginity, can be found with few. Whence: "All men take not this word, but they to whom it is given."

04_marg1789: WHATSOEVER FOR THE SERVICE etc. GREGORY. In the adorning of the tabernacle men with women offer gifts, because in completing the worship of holy Church both the lofty deeds of the strong and the least works of the weak are counted. The faith of holy Church too is compared to gold, the word of preaching to silver. But what is shown by the bracelets, which bind the arms, but the works of prelates labouring strongly? By the earrings the obedience of subjects is expressed. By the rings, the sealing of secrets; for masters often seal what they consider cannot be grasped by hearers. By the tablets, the adornments of the first working. By the vessel of gold set aside for the gifts of the Lord, the understanding of the Godhead, which is as far parted from the love of lower things as it is raised to love eternal things alone. By violet, the hope of heavenly things. By purple, blood and the endurance of sufferings shown for love of the perpetual kingdom. What by the scarlet twice dyed but charity, which is dyed twice by perfection, because it is adorned with the love of God and neighbour? What by fine linen but the spotless incorruption of the flesh? What by goats' hair, of which the roughness of haircloth is woven, but the hard affliction of penitents is signified? While then some by bracelets and rings exercise a strong mastership, others by earrings and tablets show devout obedience and right working. Others by the vessel of gold set apart hold an illustrious and subtler understanding; others by violet, purple and scarlet do not cease to hope and believe the heavenly things they have heard, even those which they do not yet know by subtler understanding. Others by fine linen offer the incorruption of the flesh. Others by goats' hair bewail harshly what they gladly committed; as if the mysteries of the gifts, joined together into one work of the craftsman, are brought forth in the tabernacle of the Lord, that is, the Church, as he himself has given.

04_marg1790: THE PRINCES OFFERED etc. ORIGEN. The princes offered their gifts, namely gems, emerald stones, stones of filling, and stones for the ephod. Those are called stones of filling which are set in the logion, that is, which are placed on the breast of the high priest, with the names of the tribes of Israel inscribed. And the logion, that is, the rational, which is placed on the breast of the high priest, has the form of the rational sense which is in us. In this are set the stones of filling, which cling and are joined to the stones of the ephod, so that from these the adornment of the bound ephod is continued, in which is the token of good acts. Action therefore is joined with reason, and reason with actions, that there may be harmony in both: He that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. Let there be in us then a word hanging on acts, and let acts adorn the word: for this is the adornment of the high priest; but for fulfilling these, princes are required. This adornment is theirs who have advanced so far that they deserve to be set over peoples.
04_marg1791: The princes also offer oil to serve for the lamps and the chrism. For the lamp of those who are set over peoples ought not to be hidden or put under a bushel, but on a candlestick, that it may shine to all that are in the house. The princes also offer the composition of the incense, which is compounded by Moses for an odour of sweetness to the Lord, that it may be said of them also: For we are the good odour of Christ.
04_marg1792: Morally. Each one can set up a tabernacle in himself. For if, as some before us have said, this tabernacle holds the figure of the whole world, and each can have the image of the world, why not also of the tabernacle? Each therefore ought to fit to himself pillars of virtues, silver pillars, that is, rational patience. For there seems to be a patience which is not rational. For he who does not feel an injury, and therefore does not repay it, seems patient, but is not rational. That patience has pillars, but not silver ones. But he who suffers bravely for the sake of the word of God is adorned with silver pillars. He can stretch out courts in himself by enlarging his heart. Whence: "Be you also enlarged." He can fortify himself with bars, namely bind himself with the unanimity of love. He can stand on silver sockets when he is set on the steadfastness of the word of God, the prophetic and apostolic word. He can have on the pillar a gilded head, that is, the faith of Christ. For "the head of every man is Christ". And he can stretch out ten courts in himself when he is enlarged not in one word only of the law, nor in two or three, but can enlarge the amplitude of spiritual understanding in the whole decalogue of the law; or when he has brought forth the fruit of the Holy Ghost: joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, modesty, faith, continence, with charity added, which is the greatest of all.
04_marg1793: Morally. Let him have an altar fixed in himself, on which he may offer the victims of prayers and the sacrifices of mercy, on which with the knife of continence he may slay pride as a bull, cut the throat of anger as a ram, and sacrifice wantonness and all lust as he-goats and kids. Let the priest know, however, how to separate from these the right shoulder, that is, good works, right works, lest anything left-handed be kept back; and the whole breast, a right heart and a devout mind consecrated to God; and the jaws, for speaking the word of God. Let him know that a candlestick of light is to be placed for him in the holy place, that he may have lamps always burning, and loins girt, that he may be as a servant who waits for his lord to return from the wedding. Of these lamps it is said: "The light of thy body is thy eye."
04_marg1794: Morally. Let him place the candlestick also in the south, so that it looks toward the north. For, the light being kindled, that is, with a watchful heart, he ought always to look toward the north, from which the evils of all the earth are kindled. Watchful therefore and careful and burning, let him always look out against the wiles of the devil, and whence temptation may come, whence the enemy may rush in, whence he may creep in secretly, who "as a roaring lion goeth about seeking whom he may devour".
04_marg1795: Morally. Let him have in the inner chambers of the breast the altar of incense, that he may say: "We are the good odour of Christ unto God."
04_marg1796: Morally. Let the table of proposition also, having twelve loaves, be placed in the north part looking toward the south: the loaves are the apostles, whose word he ought to use unceasingly, and to look toward the south, whence the Lord comes.
04_marg1797: Morally. Let him have the ark of the testament, in which are the tables of the law, that we may meditate on the law of God day and night, and his memory may be made an ark and library of the books of God. Within it too let there be laid up the pot of manna, namely the subtle and sweet understanding of the word of God. Let there be also the rod of Aaron, that is, priestly doctrine and the flowering severity of discipline. But above all glory let him have the high priest's adornment. For that part in him which is more precious than all can perform a high priesthood within him, which some call the principal part of the heart, others the rational sense or intellectual substance; or in whatever way that portion of ours is named by which we are capable of God, let it be adorned in us like a high priest with precious vestments and ornaments, with the poderis of fine linen; which vestment is drawn down to the feet, covering the whole body: in which it is signified that first of all he be wholly clothed with chastity.
04_marg1798: Morally. After this let him take the ephod set with gems, in which is the brightness of works, that seeing your good works they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.
04_marg1799: Morally. Let him take the logion, which can be called the rational, laid upon the breast, marked out by a fourfold order of stones. Let the golden plate too shine on the forehead, which is called the petalum, on both of which truth and manifestation are said to be placed. I perceive in those things placed on the breast the gospel word, which in a fourfold order sets out to us the truth of faith and the manifestation of the Trinity, referring all things to the head, that is, to the nature of one God. In these therefore is all truth and all manifestation of truth. If therefore thou wilt bear the high priesthood, let the gospel word and the faith of the Trinity always be held in thy breast, with which the apostolic word agrees both in virtue and in number; so that the name of the Lord may always be held on the head, and all things be referred to one God.
04_marg1800: Morally. Let the high priest also have his inner coverings, let him have his nakedness covered, and be holy in body and spirit, and pure in thoughts and works.
04_marg1801: Morally. Let him have also bells round the border of his vestment, that going into the holy place he may sound, and not go in with silence; and set on the edge of the vestment, that he may never be silent about the last times and the end of the world. Therefore let him sound, dispute and speak, that, mindful of his last end, he may not sin. So therefore let the inner man be adorned, that he may enter not only into the holy place but into the Holy of holies, where the propitiatory and the Cherubim are, whence God may appear to them. The Holy can be those things which holy conversation can have in the present world. But the Holy of holies, into which one enters only once, I think is the passing into heaven, where the propitiatory and the Cherubim are, where God appears to the clean of heart. As I understand it, Abraham dwelt in tabernacles, and Isaac and Jacob, which they had set up within themselves for God, who adorned themselves with so great and such splendours of virtues. Kingly purple shone in them. Whence it was said by God to Abraham: Thou art a king among us. The scarlet shone when his right hand was ready to slay Isaac, his only son, for God. And the violet, when, ever gazing on heaven, he followed the Lord of heaven. In the rest also he was likewise adorned. So it is commanded in the law that the people go out on a certain day of the year and keep the feast day of tabernacles, dwelling in tabernacles, having branches of palms and boughs of willow and poplar, and branches of a leafy tree, that is, of myrtle. The palm is the sign of victory in the war which the flesh and the spirit wage with each other. The poplar and willow trees are, both in virtue and in name, shoots of chastity: which if thou keep whole, thou canst have also the branches of the shady and leafy tree, which is eternal and blessed life, when the Lord shall have set thee in a place of pasture by the water of refreshment.

04_interl4902: There is no child of Israel who does not offer something in the tabernacle.
04_interl4903: No forced offering is received in this tabernacle.

04_interl4905: For this is the gift of God.
04_marg1802: Beseleel is called shadow. Hur: fire. Uri: my light. Juda: confession. Ooliab: my protection, father; Achisamech is interpreted 'strengthening my brother'; Dan 'judgment' or 'judging'. Because the holy doctors, who by their preaching proclaim and build the house of God, trust in God's defence. Whence: "In the shadow of thy wings will I hope" etc. And kindled with spiritual zeal they pour the light of faith and knowledge into their hearers and show the rule of confession; they have also the protection of God the father, and in justice and judgment they strengthen their brethren by exhorting them.
